title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
body_text: Recursive Self-Improvement via AI for Chip Design & Chip Design for AI - Ricursive Intelligence Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model. To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains. Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4). Rippleâs dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The modelâs small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today. Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone. In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge. Â¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run. Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.  Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA. A Co-Designed Model Architecture Ripple-65B Previewâs architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization. Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals . Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements We optimized Rippleâs pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.  Our starting point was Olmo 3âs model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.  Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale. Conclusion We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier. We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.  At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If youâre interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers . Â¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain. Â© 2026 Ricursive Intelligence, Inc.

body_text: A new Go API for JSON - The Go Programming Language Skip to Main Content Why Go arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Case Studies Common problems companies solve with Go Use Cases Stories about how and why companies use Go Security How Go can help keep you secure by default Learn Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Docs arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Go Spec The official Go language specification Go User Manual A complete introduction to building software with Go Standard library Reference documentation for Go's standard library Release Notes Learn what's new in each Go release Effective Go Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code Packages Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Community arrow_drop_down Press Enter to activate/deactivate dropdown Recorded Talks Videos from prior events Meetups open_in_new Meet other local Go developers Conferences open_in_new Learn and network with Go developers from around the world Go blog The Go project's official blog. Go project Get help and stay informed from Go Get connected Why Go navigate_next navigate_before Why Go Case Studies Use Cases Security Learn Docs navigate_next navigate_before Docs Go Spec Go User Manual Standard library Release Notes Effective Go Packages Community navigate_next navigate_before Community Recorded Talks Meetups open_in_new Conferences open_in_new Go blog Go project Get connected The Go Blog A new Go API for JSON Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026 Introduction JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago! Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes. After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages. Problems with encoding/json Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings. Behavior flaws There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json : Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream. encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names. Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default. Case-insensitive unmarshaling : When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation. Inconsistent calling of methods : Due to an implementation detail, MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by encoding/json . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior. API deficiencies The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive: It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v) , which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input. Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types, but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions. Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method. The Compact , Indent , and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer . This limits the usability of those functions. Performance limitations Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations: MarshalJSON : The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned []byte . Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation. UnmarshalJSON : The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON . Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again. Lack of streaming : Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens. Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function, then the performance becomes quadratic. Trying to fix encoding/json directly Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package. While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise . We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2 , but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package. This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2 ), where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1 ). Building on encoding/json/jsontext Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the encoding/json/jsontext package that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go. JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components: syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values. We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling. This diagram provides an overview of this separation. Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods. The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data. The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package, contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax, while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package, contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data handled by the bottom half. The basic API of jsontext is the following: package jsontext type Encoder struct { ... } func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error type Decoder struct { ... } func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error) func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error) type Kind byte type Value []byte func (Value) Kind() Kind type Token struct { ... } func (Token) Kind() Kind The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON at a syntactic level and derives its name from RFC 8259, section 2 where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text . Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level, it does not depend on Go reflection. The Encoder and Decoder provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens. The constructors accept variadic options that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding. Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1 , the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner. A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as a named []byte . It is identical to RawMessage in v1 , which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value . A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens. A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type with constructors and accessor methods. It is analogous to Token in v1 but is designed represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation. To resolve the fundamental performance problems with the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods, we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON as a streaming sequence of tokens and values. In v2 , we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods that operate on an Encoder or Decoder , allowing the methods’ implementations to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON , nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value provided to UnmarshalJSON . These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder . Introducing encoding/json/v2 Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the encoding/json/v2 package. It is designed to fix the problems in v1 , while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package. Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2 . Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2 . For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to study the examples in the v2 package , the “ Working with JSON ” tutorial, or read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic . The basic API of v2 is the following: package json func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error) func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error The Marshal and Unmarshal functions have a signature similar to v1 , but accept options to configure their behavior. The MarshalWrite and UnmarshalRead functions directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder just to write or read from such types. The MarshalEncode and UnmarshalDecode functions operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and is actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions. Unlike v1 , options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions, greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2 . There are several options available in v2 which are not covered by this article. Type-specified customization Similar to v1 , v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation by satisfying particular interfaces. type Marshaler interface { MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) } type MarshalerTo interface { MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error } type Unmarshaler interface { UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error } type UnmarshalerFrom interface { UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error } The Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces are identical to those in v1 . The new MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder . This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder . See the OrderedObject example for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members. Caller-specified customization In v2 , the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type, where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods or the default representation for a particular type. func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options type Marshalers struct { ... } func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options type Unmarshalers struct { ... } func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers MarshalFunc and MarshalToFunc construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types. Similarly, UnmarshalFunc and UnmarshalFromFunc support similar customization for Unmarshal . The ProtoJSON example demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all proto.Message types to be handled by the protojson package. Behavior differences While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1 , its behavior has changed in some ways to address problems in v1 , most notably: v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8. v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name. v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively. v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name. v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null , "" , [] , and {} ). v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration , which currently has no default representation , but provides options to let the caller decide. For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics, or even other caller-determined behavior. See “ Migrating to v2 ” for more information. Performance optimizations The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1 . Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower. The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1 , with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x. In order to obtain greater performance gains, existing implementations of Marshaler and Unmarshaler should migrate to also implement MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom , so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner. For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes (see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315 ), while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude. For more benchmark details, see the go-json-experiment/jsonbench repository. On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1 . You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28. Compatibility The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go. The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise. Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2 . That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported. We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together. Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies. For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package. That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior. No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected. Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct. The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance. No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2 ’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood. We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2 . As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options . Each behavior difference is controlled by one of the these options. Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options. With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo ) or new struct tags (e.g., embed ) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users. Migration Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites. encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2 , and which option controls that behaviors. Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on. For example, we can select all v2 behavior except for allowing duplicate names: json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(true)) Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except for disallowing duplicate names: json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateName(false)) The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2 . More information For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see: The “ Working with JSON ” tutorial, The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation, The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation, and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide . A long time coming The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years. In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package, Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json ) first drafted his thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like . Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers , Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the Protocol Buffer specification required, nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner. Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable, Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and started to build a prototype (with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module). Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt) joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing. Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our recorded meetings and meeting notes . Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes . This work has been public since the beginning, and we increasingly involved the wider Go community, first with a GopherCon talk and discussion posted in late 2023 , formal proposal posted in early 2025 , and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25 for wider-scale testing by all Go users. The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point, incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable empirical experience from use in production settings. It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem. Thank you to everyone that contributed! CREATE AN ACCOUNT SIGN IN Computing News The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt Dina Genkina 02 Nov 2026 4 min read Dina Genkina is the computing and hardware editor at IEEE Spectrum iStock In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server. As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI. “One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.” PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed. “If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University . “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately. Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.” AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible. “There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.” This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models . “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.” Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.” Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green , an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.” In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.” One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.” From Your Site Articles Your AI Agent Is Now a Target for Email Phishing › With $1 Cyberattacks on the Rise, Durable Defenses Pay Off › What Anthropic’s Mythos Means for the Future of Cybersecurity › Related Articles Around the Web The PHP Foundation — The PHP Foundation — Supporting, Advancing, and Developing the PHP Language › cybersecurity internet artificial intelligence Dina Genkina Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. She holds a PhD in atomic physics and lives in Brooklyn. External-model trajectories that retrieve reference answers online receive zero for those tasks. Frontier Finance. Evaluated with the official Finance Agent v2 harness. HANDBOOK.md. Evaluated with the official OpenHands-based harness, using tasks from the benchmark's early open-source v1 release. Harvey Legal Agent. Evaluated on 1,251 public tasks with Artificial Analysis's Stirrup harness. The reported score is the all-pass rate: the percentage of tasks passing every rubric criterion. OSWorld V2.1. Kimi models use the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repository. GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report. DECK-Arena and Design Bench. DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries; Design Bench covers graphic design through direct and reference-image few-shot prompting. Both evaluate python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation. The automated grader is calibrated on more than 10,000 human judgments. BrowseComp. Uses context compaction triggered at 200K tokens and a 500-step maximum. If the limit is reached, the agent is forced to answer before judging. All runs use temperature = 1.0 and top-p = 1.0 . GDPval-AA v2.1, AA-Briefcase v1.1, and AutomationBench-AA. Scores are cited from Artificial Analysis . APEX-Agents. Scores are cited from the official leaderboard . Tool-augmented multimodal evaluations. GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python, and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks with Python are averaged over four. For GDP.pdf w/ python, each original PDF is sent to a sandbox for IPython processing. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash at medium reasoning effort and the official judging prompt. The reported score is the task-macro mean rubric pass rate. Reasoning, knowledge, and multimodal benchmarks GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. The table reports the strict pass rate among fully scored responses. GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max scores are cited from Artificial Analysis . HLE-Full and HLE-Diamond. The full evaluation sets contain 2,500 and 1,000 questions, respectively. For scores marked * , accuracy is reported on the text-only subset. Run counts. GDP.pdf, ZeroBench, and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs; other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four. MMMU-Pro. Evaluated using the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input. PerceptionBench. An in-house benchmark focused on atomic visual perception capabilities. Kimi Hallucination Benchmark. Evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. The table reports claim-level hallucination rates assessed by fact-checking agents. Cybersecurity benchmarks ExploitBench. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the official harness under a 300-turn budget. The table reports the pass@5 maximum-capability score: for each environment, the best of five seeds is scored by capability flags reached out of 16; arbitrary code execution counts as all 16 capabilities. Comparison scores are from OpenAI , Anthropic , and GLM-5.3 . ExploitGym. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code under a six-hour wall-clock budget per task. GPT-6 Astra, Claude, and GLM comparison scores are taken from their respective official reports, with Claude results using the same six-hour budget. xdev-bench-hard. K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Kimi Code; GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 use Claude Code. The internal benchmark contains expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks. The final model is evaluated at pass@3 over a random subset of runs, without hard timeouts or output-token limits. 4. Deployment and Availability You can access Kimi K3.1 Pro's API on https://platform.kimi.ai by selecting kimi-k3.1-pro , and we provide OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API for you. Currently, Kimi K3.1 Pro is recommended to run on the following inference engines: vLLM — see recipes SGLang — see cookbook TokenSpeed — see recipes 5. Model Usage The thinking effort of Kimi K3.1 Pro is configured with the top-level reasoning_effort request field, which supports "low" , "high" , and "max" (default "max" ). For multi-turn conversations and tool calls, Kimi K3.1 Pro requires the complete assistant message returned by the API to be passed back to messages as-is — including reasoning_content and tool_calls , not just content : import openai def chat_with_preserved_thinking ( client: openai.OpenAI, model_name: str ): messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Tell me three random numbers." }, { "role" : "assistant" , "reasoning_content" : "I'll start by listing five numbers: 473, 921, 235, 215, 222, and I'll tell you the first three." , "content" : "473, 921, 235" }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What are the other two numbers you have in mind?" } ] response = client.chat.completions.create( model=model_name, messages=messages, stream= False , max_tokens= 4096 , reasoning_effort= "max" , ) # the assistant should mention 215 and 222 that appear in the prior reasoning content print ( f"response: {response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning} " ) return response.choices[ 0 ].message.content For full guides and examples (vision input, structured output, partial mode, tool choice, dynamic tool loading, context caching), see the Kimi K3.1 Pro Quickstart and Thinking Effort . 6. If you do not agree to be bound by the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy, you may not use the 99% Invisible website and services. see recent newsletter Close Article by Kurt Kohlstedt Guerrilla Bike Lanes: San Francisco Makes Illicit Infrastructure Permanent Image via the SFMTrA Click to enlarge image Infrastructure Category Infrastructure Date 11.14.16 Producer Kurt Kohlstedt Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Leave a Comment When two cyclists were tragically  killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such  guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by  making the change official . Image by Nicasio Nakamine The SFMTrA , a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including: Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians. Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists. Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety. Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones , which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive. Image via the SFMTrA “Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement , “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete. Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group  Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts. Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation  would put the delineators back in place. In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane). 99% Invisible Guerrilla Public Service Redux Episode 288 Guerrilla Public Service Redux Play Pause Add to Queue Remove from Queue Download Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also  jailed or fined  by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress . Trending RTX Spark Deals Nova Lake RAM Shortage AI Data Centers TH App RAM Combo Deals Vera Rubin Tom's 30th Anniversary PC Components CPUs AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history — $17B guidance would exceed Intel's projections News By Anton Shilov Published 4 November 2026 AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027 When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . (Image credit: AMD) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 14 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds. As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history. Image 1 of 2 (Image credit: AMD) (Image credit: AMD) Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%. (Image credit: AMD) The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft , OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems. You may like Desktop CPU shipments crater 20% amid high component costs, but AMD gains record share despite 'ugly' desktop processor market Intel shifts production capacity from consumer to server CPUs in face of 'unprecedented' AI demand Nvidia revenue tops $96 billion as memory commitments soar to $160 billion AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025. "We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth." Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter. (Image credit: AMD) Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago. Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%. What to read next AMD beats Intel to the trillion-dollar club as stock price soars Intel reportedly set to hike CPU prices by 10% ahead of 'major annual product' launch in March 2027 Nvidia expects to sell $20 billion worth of Vera Rubin hardware this quarter "In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint." AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027. Embedded business strong, set to accelerate As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers. (Image credit: AMD) AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years. "Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year." Beating Intel For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint. In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints. (Image credit: AMD) If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead. The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages. I know that in the scheme of things home users are small change and that businesses are the target but that time was when AMD were incredibly vulnerable, all their cards were on the table, intel was still ahead and people had to have faith in a brand new untested product. In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach. “Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” REG AD Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group , known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists . The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers , who are then hired by Western companies , and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices . REG AD With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter. The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation . While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says. Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened.  In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.”  The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities. According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware. Here’s the script: CREATE  /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_   REG AD MODIFY  pyenv_ → 3,414 B   DELETE  .../libexec/pyenv  (3,344 B)      ← remove the valid pyenv RENAME  pyenv_ → pyenv  (3,414 B)  ← replace it with a malicious version DELETE  /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv  (3,414 B) ln  (create a new symlink)  +  spawn zsh Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C. Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack. As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets. REG AD The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. body_text: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts) | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts) 631 points by jameslk 16 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 164 comments If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information . https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988 “[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“ https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review “A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data “Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage “Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.” To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours. I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough. Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424   help fny 11 hours ago | next [–] "These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers." PSA: This is true of all the frontier model providers even if you disable activity tracking. They are all constantly monitoring your interactions for problematic behavior. title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
body_text: Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works | MindStudio Skip to main content Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Blog / Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works RTX Spark Linux Nvidia DGX Spark Linux dual boot laptop Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works A hands-on look at dual-booting Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, the GPU clock throttling bug found, and why WSL still wins. Edited by Luis Chavez-Mattos , Director of Product · November 1, 2026 · RSS Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop? Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read. TL;DR Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly. A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown. GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in , compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it. Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly : Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9. Memory allocation is a separate headache , since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today , since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM. A real fix depends on Nvidia , specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark. Self-host Remy. On-prem or in your private cloud. Remy and every app you build stay inside your walls. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC? The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM. That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place. Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance. How do you actually install Linux on it? The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot. Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel. Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration. Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps. How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL? This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower. Every team builds with AI. Nothing gets lost. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed. Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power. Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down? The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line. Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back. The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver. Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now? For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs. The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly. Frequently Asked Questions Can the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop dual-boot Windows and Linux? Yes. Dual-booting was demonstrated on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop using Omarchy, a Linux distribution that already included Nvidia’s open kernel driver for this chip, after an initial attempt with Debian required manual driver and networking workarounds. Why is Linux so much slower than Windows on this laptop when plugged in? Developers have their tools. Enterprises have Remy. Developers > add rate limiting to the API ● Reading src/server.ts ● Editing 3 files + import { limit } from 'rate' - app.use(cors()) ✓ Tests passed · ready for PR Enterprises Loan Approvals ● Live SOC 2 Role-based access Self-hosted Mortgage · $412,000 Approved Small business · $85,000 Approved Auto · $31,500 Approved The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today A Windows-only firmware component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power sharing between the CPU and GPU. Without a Linux equivalent, the GPU’s clock speed gets locked around 780 MHz when the laptop is connected to power, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows. Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem? It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect. Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark? Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM. Will Nvidia fix Linux GPU performance on RTX Spark laptops? That depends on Nvidia shipping the platform controller’s power management logic in its Linux driver. The encrypted firmware power table currently can only be decrypted by Windows, and no workaround found so far restores full clock speed on Linux without it.
