¶ kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast , GPU based terminal. To update kitty , follow the instructions . Recent major new features ¶ Docked windows [0.50] ¶ kitty windows can now be docked to an edge of another window or of the tab. Docked windows are placed outside the layout, making them perfect for status bars, file trees or a shell kept next to your editor. A dock attached to a window follows it around, moving with it to other tabs and closing when it closes. Create docks with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock . Docks are saved in sessions too. Restore after logout [0.50] ¶ Like other applications, kitty can now save its state when you log out, restart or shut down your computer, and restore it the next time it starts. Simply set restore_session_after_logout and every kitty instance comes back with all its OS Windows, tabs and windows in place, including their scrollback. On macOS, the saved state is encrypted using a key stored in your keychain. See Restoring kitty after logging out for details. Custom shaders [0.49] ¶ kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders . These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised. See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty. Performance improvements [0.49] ¶ This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details: Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+). Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD , filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives. Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped Vertical tabs [0.48] ¶ kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows. Drag and drop for terminal programs [0.47] ¶ kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program. Mousing [0.46] ¶ kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for smooth scrolling and momentum based scrolling for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience. Additionally, you can now drag kitty tabs around with the mouse to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into their own OS Window. Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented. Choose files, fast [0.45] ¶ A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text. On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs. Sessions [0.43] ¶ kitty has long had support for Sessions , aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file , for seamless and intuitive session file creation. A scrollbar for the kitty scrollback [0.43] ¶ A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is extensively configurable in kitty.conf. Note that the old scrollback_indicator_opacity option is deprecated. Multiple cursors [0.43] ¶ kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last. Access kitty with a single keypress [0.42] ¶ Screenshots macOS ¶ Linux ¶ A sample panel on Linux ¶ How the screenshots were generated . kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress. See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up . Multiple sized text [0.40] ¶ kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol . Cursor trails [0.37] ¶ Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be turned on by the cursor_trail option in kitty.conf . Variable font support [0.36] ¶ Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports OpenType Variable fonts . These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization abilities, such as: symbol_map , text_composition_strategy , font_features and modify_font . kitty knows text rendering is important, and goes the extra mile for it. Desktop notifications [0.36] ¶ kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features. Wayland goodies [0.34] ¶ Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements: Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor. Detailed list of changes ¶ 0.50.0 [2026-11-03] ¶ Allow docking kitty windows to the edges of other windows or of the tab, for status bars, file trees, etc. Create them with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock , see Docked windows A new option restore_session_after_logout to save the state of every kitty instance, including scrollback, when logging out, restarting or shutting down and restore it the next time kitty starts. On macOS, the state is encrypted with a key in the keychain. On Linux, it requires the Inhibit desktop portal. See Restoring kitty after logging out ( #1197 , #10659 ) Allow using tabs like named workspaces: A new launch --focus-existing option to focus an existing window or tab instead of creating a new one, a new by-title value for launch --location to keep tabs in alphabetical order and new options for kitten @ detach-window and the detach_window action to send windows to a named tab, creating it if needed ( #10627 ) Wayland: The client side window decorations used on compositors such as GNOME now look like native GNOME decorations and follow the desktop titlebar font, text scaling, button layout and titlebar click action settings ( #10766 ) Wayland: Support touchscreens. A tap is a click, a finger that moves scrolls with momentum, and a finger held still before it moves selects text ( #5432 , #10551 ) Custom shaders: New cursor-trail-railgun , cursor-trail-torpedo and cursor-trail-pixiedust shaders that make particles fly off the cursor as it moves, in the style of neovide. Shaders can now be controlled with key presses via the new shader_event action (see Controlling shaders with key presses ), can be faded in and out, reversed and looped with new animation_* pipeline directives and can define a pointer_map() function so that clicks and selections land on the text shown under the mouse, which the crt shader now uses, see Shaders that move content . Also fix animations becoming jerky after kitty has been running for a few hours, shaders specified by path not being found and various pipeline bugs ( #10587 , #10667 , #10693 , #10595 , #10694 , #10639 ) Graphics protocol: Add two new indexed color image formats whose pixels are indices into the terminal color palette, so that images change color along with the color scheme, and allow clients to detect support for individual protocol features, such as animation and Unicode placeholders, via the new e query key, see Querying support for protocol features ( #9379 , #10732 ) Support the Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) that lets programs report whether they are working, finished, failed or blocked waiting on the user. See tab_bar_style and tab_fade for details. The old look can be restored by setting tab_bar_style to separator . Pre-compiled binaries with all bundled dependencies for Linux ( #595 ) A new kitten to create dock panels on X11 desktops showing the output from arbitrary terminal programs. Reduce data sent to the GPU per render by 30% ( commit: 8dea5b3e3 ) Implement changing the font size for individual top level (OS) windows ( #408 ) When viewing the scrollback in less using ctrl+shift+h and kitty is currently scrolled, position the scrollback in less to match kitty’s scroll position. ( #148 ) ssh kitten: Support all SSH options. It can now be aliased directly to ssh for convenience. ( #591 ) icat kitten: Add kitty +kitten icat --print-window-size to easily detect the window size in pixels from scripting languages ( #581 ) hints kitten: Allow selecting hashes from the terminal with ctrl+shift+p>h useful for git commits. ( #604 ) Allow specifying initial window size in number of cells in addition to pixels ( #436 ) Add a setting to control the margins to the left and right of the tab-bar ( #584 ) When closing a tab switch to the last active tab instead of the right-most tab ( #585 ) Wayland: Fix kitty not starting when using wl_roots based compositors ( #157 ) Wayland: Fix mouse wheel/touchpad scrolling in opposite direction to other apps ( #594 ) macOS: Fix the new OS window keyboard shortcut ( ctrl+shift+n ) not working if no kitty window currently has focus. ( #524 ) macOS: Keep kitty running even when the last window is closed. This is in line with how applications are supposed to behave on macOS ( #543 ). There is a new option ( macos_quit_when_last_window_closed ) to control this. macOS: Add macOS standard shortcuts for copy, paste and new OS window (⌘+C, ⌘+V, ⌘+N) Add a config option ( editor ) to set the EDITOR kitty uses ( #580 ) Add a config option ( x11_hide_window_decorations ) to hide window decorations under X11/Wayland ( #607 ) Add an option to @set-window-title to make the title change non-permanent ( #592 ) Add support for the CSI t escape code to query window and cell sizes ( #581 ) Linux: When using layouts that map the keys to non-ascii characters, map shortcuts using the ascii equivalents, from the default layout. ( #606 ) Linux: Fix fonts not being correctly read from TrueType Collection (.ttc) files ( #577 ) Fix inactive_text_alpha also applying to the tab bar ( #612 ) hints kitten : Fix a regression that caused some blank lines to be not be displayed. Linux: Include a man page and the HTML docs when building the linux-package Remote control: Fix kitty @ sometimes failing to read the response from kitty. ( #614 ) Fix kitty @ set-colors not working with the window border colors. ( #623 ) Fix a regression in 0.10 that caused incorrect rendering of the status bar in irssi when used inside screen. ( #621 ) 0.10.1 [2018-05-24] ¶ Add a kitten to easily ssh into servers that automatically copies the terminfo files over. kitty +kitten ssh myserver . diff kitten: Make the keyboard shortcuts configurable ( #563 ) Allow controlling background_opacity via either keyboard shortcuts or remote control. Note that you must set dynamic_background_opacity yes in kitty.conf first. ( #569 ) diff kitten: Add keybindings to scroll by page diff kitten: Fix incorrect syntax highlighting for a few file formats such as yaml macOS: Fix regression that caused the macos_option_as_alt setting to always be disabled for all OS windows in a kitty instance after the first window ( #571 ) Fix Ctrl+Alt+Space not working in normal and application keyboard modes ( #562 ) 0.10.0 [2018-05-21] ¶ A diff kitten to show side-by-side diffs with syntax highlighting and support for images. See diff kitten . Make windows in the various kitty layouts manually resizable. See Layouts for details. Implement support for the SGR faint escape code to make text blend into the background ( #446 ). Make the hints kitten a little smarter ( commit: ad1109b6f ) so that URLs that stretch over multiple lines are detected. Also improve detection of surrounding brackets/quotes. Make the kitty window id available as the environment variable KITTY_WINDOW_ID ( #532 ). Add a “fat” layout that is similar to the “tall” layout but vertically oriented. Expand environment variables in config file include directives Allow programs running in kitty to read/write from the clipboard ( commit: 889ca7791 ). By default only writing is allowed. This feature is supported in many terminals, search for OSC 52 clipboard to find out more about using it. Fix moving cursor outside a defined page area incorrectly causing the cursor to be placed inside the page area. Caused incorrect rendering in neovim, in some situations ( #542 ). Render a couple more powerline symbols directly, bypassing the font ( #550 ). Fix ctrl+alt+<special> not working in normal and application keyboard ( #548 ). Partial fix for rendering Right-to-left languages like Arabic. Rendering of Arabic is never going to be perfect, but now it is at least readable. Fix Ctrl+backspace acting as plain backspace in normal and application keyboard modes ( #538 ). Have the paste_from_selection action paste from the clipboard on platforms that do not have a primary selection such as Wayland and macOS ( #529 ) Fix cursor_stop_blinking_after=0 not working ( #530 ) 0.9.1 [2018-05-05] ¶ Show a bell symbol on the tab if a bell occurs in one of the windows in the tab and the window is not the currently focused window Change the window border color if a bell occurs in an unfocused window. Can be disabled by setting the bell_border_color to be the same as the inactive_border_color. macOS: Add support for dead keys Unicode input: When searching by name search for prefix matches as well as whole word matches Dynamically allocate the memory used for the scrollback history buffer. Reduces startup memory consumption when using very large scrollback buffer sizes. Add an option to not request window attention on bell. Remote control: Allow matching windows by number (visible position). macOS: Fix changing tab title and kitty shell not working When triple-clicking select all wrapped lines belonging to a single logical line. hints kitten: Detect bracketed URLs and don’t include the closing bracket in the URL. When calling pass_selection_to_program use the current directory of the child process as the cwd of the program. Add macos_hide_from_tasks option to hide kitty from the macOS task switcher macOS: When the macos_titlebar_color is set to background change the titlebar colors to match the current background color of the active kitty window Add a setting to clear all shortcuts defined up to that point in the config file(s) Add a setting (kitty_mod) to change the modifier used by all the default kitty shortcuts, globally Fix Shift+function key not working Support the F13 to F25 function keys Don’t fail to start if the user deletes the hintstyle key from their fontconfig configuration. When rendering a private use unicode codepoint and a space as a two cell ligature, set the foreground colors of the space cell to match the colors of the first cell. Works around applications like powerline that use different colors for the two cells. Fix passing @text to other programs such as when viewing the scrollback buffer not working correctly if kitty is itself scrolled up. Fix window focus gained/lost events not being reported to child programs when switching windows/tabs using the various keyboard shortcuts. Fix tab title not changing to reflect the window title when switching between different windows in a tab Ignore -e if it is specified on the command line. This is for compatibility with broken software that assumes terminals should run with an -e option to execute commands instead of just passing the commands as arguments. 0.9.0 [2018-04-15] ¶ A new kitty command shell to allow controlling kitty via commands. Press ctrl+shift+escape to run the shell. The hints kitten has become much more powerful. Now in addition to URLs you can use it to select word, paths, filenames, lines, etc. from the screen. These can be inserted into the terminal, copied to clipboard or sent to external programs. Linux: Switch to libxkbcommon for keyboard handling. It allows kitty to support XCompose and dead keys and also react to keyboard remapping/layout change without needing a restart. Add support for multiple-key-sequence shortcuts A new remote control command set-colors to change the current and/or configured colors. When double-clicking to select a word, select words that continue onto the next/prev line as well. Add an include directive for the config files to read multiple config files Improve mouse selection for windows with padding. Moving the mouse into the padding area now acts as if the mouse is over the nearest cell. Allow setting all 256 terminal colors in the config file Fix using kitty --single-instance to open a new window in a running kitty instance, not respecting the --directory flag URL hints: Exclude trailing punctuation from URLs URL hints: Launch the browser from the kitty parent process rather than the hints kitten. Fixes launching on some systems where xdg-open doesn’t like being run from a kitten. Allow using rectangle select mode by pressing shift in addition to the rectangle select modifiers even when the terminal program has grabbed the mouse. 0.8.4 [2018-03-31] ¶ Fix presence of XDG_CONFIG_DIRS and absence of XDG_CONFIG_HOME preventing kitty from starting Revert change in last release to cell width calculation. Instead just clip the right edges of characters that overflow the cell by at most two pixels 0.8.3 [2018-03-29] ¶ Fix a regression that broke the visual bell and invert screen colors escape code Allow double-click and triple-click + drag to extend selections word at a time or line at a time Add a keyboard shortcut to set the tab title Fix setting window title to empty via OSC escape code not working correctly Linux: Fix cell width calculation incorrect for some fonts (cell widths are now calculated by actually rendering bitmaps, which is slower but more accurate) Allow specifying a system wide kitty config file, for all users Add a --debug-config command line flag to output data about the system and kitty configuration. Wayland: Fix auto-repeat of keys not working 0.8.2 [2018-03-17] ¶ Allow extending existing selections by right clicking Add a configurable keyboard shortcut and remote command to set the font size to a specific value Add an option to have kitty close the window when the main processes running in it exits, even if there are still background processes writing to that terminal Add configurable keyboard shortcuts to switch to a specific layout Add a keyboard shortcut to edit the kitty config file easily macOS: Fix restoring of window size not correct on Retina screens macOS: Add a facility to specify command line arguments when running kitty from the GUI Add a focus-tab remote command Fix screen not being refreshed immediately after moving a window. Fix a crash when getting the contents of the scrollback buffer as text 0.8.1 [2018-03-09] ¶ Extend kitty’s remote control feature to work over both UNIX and TCP sockets, so now you can control kitty from across the internet, if you want to. Render private use unicode characters that are followed by a space as a two character ligature. This fixes rendering for applications that misuse private-use characters to display square symbols. Fix Unicode emoji presentation variant selector causing new a fallback font instance to be created Fix a rare error that prevented the Unicode input kitten from working sometimes Allow using Ctrl+Alt+letter in legacy keyboard modes by outputting them as Ctrl+letter and Alt+letter. This matches other terminals’ behavior. Fix cursor position off-by-one on horizontal axis when resizing the terminal Wayland: Fix auto-repeat of keys not working Wayland: Add support for window decorations provided by the Wayland shell macOS: Fix URL hints not working macOS: Fix shell not starting in login mode on some computers macOS: Output errors into console.app when running as a bundle 0.8.0 [2018-02-24] ¶ A framework for kittens, that is, small terminal programs designed to run inside kitty and extend its capabilities. Examples include unicode input and selecting URLs with the keyboard. Input arbitrary unicode characters by pressing Ctrl+Shift+u. You can choose characters by name, by hex code, by recently used, etc. There is even and editable Favorites list. Open URLs using only the keyboard. kitty has a new “hints mode”. Press Ctrl+Shift+e and all detected URLs on the screen are highlighted with a key to press to open them. The facility is customizable so you can change what is detected as a URL and which program is used to open it. Add an option to change the titlebar color of kitty windows on macOS Only consider Emoji characters with default Emoji presentation to be two cells wide. This matches the standard. Also add support for the Unicode Emoji variation presentation selector. Prevent video tearing during high speed scrolling by syncing draws to the monitor’s refresh rate. There is a new configuration option to control this sync_to_monitor . When displaying only a single window, use the default background color of the window (which can be changed via escape codes) as the color for the margin and padding of the window. Add some non standard terminfo capabilities used by neovim and tmux. Fix large drop in performance when using multiple top-level windows on macOS Fix save/restore of window sizes not working correctly. Remove option to use system wcwidth(). Now always use a wcwidth() based on the Unicode standard. Only sane way. Fix a regression that caused a few ligature glyphs to not render correctly in rare circumstances. Browsing the scrollback buffer now happens in an overlay window instead of a new window/tab. 0.7.1 [2018-01-31] ¶ Add an option to adjust the width of character cells Fix selecting text with the mouse in the scrollback buffer selecting text from the line above the actually selected line Fix some italic fonts having the right edge of characters cut-off, unnecessarily 0.7.0 [2018-01-24] ¶ Allow controlling kitty from the shell prompt/scripts. You can open/close/rename windows and tabs and even send input to specific windows. See the README for details. Add option to put tab bar at the top instead of the bottom Add option to override the default shell Add “Horizontal” and “Vertical” window layouts Sessions: Allow setting titles and working directories for individual windows Option to copy to clipboard on mouse select Fix incorrect reporting of mouse move events when using the SGR protocol Make alt+backspace delete the previous word Take the mouse wheel multiplier option in to account when generating fake key scroll events macOS: Fix closing top-level window does not transfer focus to other top-level windows. macOS: Fix alt+arrow keys not working when disabling the macos_option_as_alt config option. kitty icat: Workaround for bug in ImageMagick that would cause some images to fail to display at certain sizes. Fix rendering of text with ligature fonts that do not use dummy glyphs Fix a regression that caused copying of the selection to clipboard to only copy the visible part of the selection Fix incorrect handling of some unicode combining marks that are not re-ordered Fix handling on non-BMP combining characters Drop the dependency on libunistring 0.6.1 [2017-12-28] ¶ Add an option to fade the text in inactive windows Add new actions to open windows/tabs/etc. with the working directory set to the working directory of the current window. Automatically adjust cell size when DPI changes, for example when kitty is moved from one monitor to another with a different DPI Ensure underlines are rendered even for fonts with very poor metrics Fix some emoji glyphs not colored on Linux Internal wcwidth() implementation is now auto-generated from the unicode standard database Allow configuring the modifiers to use for rectangular selection with the mouse. Fix incorrect minimum wayland version in the build script Fix a crash when detecting a URL that ends at the end of the line Fix regression that broke drawing of hollow cursor when window loses focus 0.6.0 [2017-12-18] ¶ Support background transparency via the background_opacity option. Provided that your OS/window manager supports transparency, you can now have kitty render pixels that have only the default background color as semi-transparent. Support multiple top level (OS) windows. These windows all share the sprite texture cache on the GPU, further reducing overall resource usage. Use the shortcut ctrl+shift+n to open a new top-level window. Add support for a daemon mode using the --single-instance command line option. With this option you can have only a single kitty instance running. All future invocations simply open new top-level windows in the existing instance. Support colored emoji Use CoreText instead of FreeType to render text on macOS Support running on the “low power” GPU on dual GPU macOS machines Add a new “grid” window layout Drop the dependency on glfw (kitty now uses a modified, bundled copy of glfw) Add an option to control the audio bell volume on X11 systems Add a command line switch to set the name part of the WM_CLASS window property independently. Add a command line switch to set the window title. Add more options to customize the tab-bar’s appearance (font styles and separator) Allow drag and drop of files into kitty. On drop kitty will paste the file path to the running program. Add an option to control the underline style for URL highlighting on hover X11: Set the WINDOWID environment variable Fix middle and right buttons swapped when sending mouse events to child processes Allow selecting in a rectangle by holding down Ctrl+Alt while dragging with the mouse. 0.5.1 [2017-12-01] ¶ Add an option to control the thickness of lines in box drawing characters Increase max. allowed ligature length to nine characters Fix text not vertically centered when adjusting line height Fix unicode block characters not being rendered properly Fix shift+up/down not generating correct escape codes Image display: Fix displaying images taller than two screen heights not scrolling properly 0.5.0 [2017-11-19] ¶ Add support for ligature fonts such as Fira Code, Hasklig, etc. kitty now uses harfbuzz for text shaping which allow it to support advanced OpenType features such as contextual alternates/ligatures/combining glyphs/etc. Make it easy to select fonts by allowing listing of monospace fonts using: kitty list-fonts Add an option to have window focus follow mouse Add a keyboard shortcut (ctrl+shift+f11) to toggle fullscreen mode macOS: Fix handling of option key. It now behaves just like the alt key on Linux. There is an option to make it type unicode characters instead. Linux: Add support for startup notification on X11 desktops. kitty will now inform the window manager when its startup is complete. Fix shell prompt being duplicated when window is resized Fix crash when displaying more than 64 images in the same session Add support for colons in SGR color codes. These are generated by some applications such as neovim when they mistakenly identify kitty as a libvte based terminal. Fix mouse interaction not working in apps using obsolete mouse interaction protocols Linux: no longer require glew as a dependency 0.4.2 [2017-10-23] ¶ Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke custom key mappings Fix a regression in 0.4.0 that broke support for non-QWERTY keyboard layouts Avoid using threads to reap zombie child processes. Also prevent kitty from hanging if the open program hangs when clicking on a URL. 0.4.0 [2017-10-22] ¶ Support for drawing arbitrary raster graphics (images) in the terminal via a new graphics protocol. kitty can draw images with full 32-bit color using both ssh connections and files/shared memory (when available) for better performance. The drawing primitives support alpha blending and z-index. Images can be drawn both above and below text. See Terminal graphics protocol . for details. Refactor kitty’s internals to make it even faster and more efficient. The CPU usage of kitty + X server while doing intensive tasks such as scrolling a file continuously in less has been reduced by 50%. There are now two configuration options repaint_delay and input_delay you can use to fine tune kitty’s performance vs CPU usage profile. The CPU usage of kitty + X when scrolling in less is now significantly better than most (all?) other terminals. See Performance . Hovering over URLs with the mouse now underlines them to indicate they can be clicked. Hold down Ctrl+Shift while clicking to open the URL. Selection using the mouse is now more intelligent. It does not add blank cells (i.e. cells that have no content) after the end of text in a line to the selection. The block cursor in now fully opaque but renders the character under it in the background color, for enhanced visibility. Allow combining multiple independent actions into a single shortcut Add a new shortcut to pass the current selection to an external program Allow creating shortcuts to open new windows running arbitrary commands. You can also pass the current selection to the command as an arguments and the contents of the screen + scrollback buffer as stdin to the command. title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
body_text: Verification Is Not Knowledge Cosmos Institute Subscribe Sign in Verification Is Not Knowledge Science needs more than answers Cosmos Institute and Jessica Hullman Oct 30, 2026 52 6 14 Share This is a guest essay by Jessica Hullman , Ginni Rometty Professor of Computer Science and Policy Fellow at Northwestern University. Diego Velázquez, The Fable of Arachne (c.1657) In his essay on the role that rigorous proofs play in mathematical advances, Bill Thurston writes that the measure of success in math research is “whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics.” Many recent discussions of AI for science hinge on a tension between understanding and answers. Is science about humans achieving insight, or the archiving of verifiable solutions? One side prioritizes outputs. Progress is implied to be evident in verifiable proofs of longstanding conjectures and cures for diseases, whether humans were involved in their making or not. The other side argues that human understanding is paramount, because it drives integration of new findings into the canon, because it shapes and inspires the next generation, and so on. But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia. When Terry Tao posed a thought experiment in a recent talk , asking how comfortable people would be taking a cancer treatment produced by AI, complete with a formal certificate of correctness and a passed phase 3 trial, but without any human understanding how it was found, critics suggested that Tao’s reasoning missed the point. Of course a patient with stage 4 cancer would welcome the treatment. Other examples concern ambiguity in authorship. Tom Dietterich wrote about arXiv’s growing problem with papers submitted by human authors who seem unlikely to have the expertise to understand the claims. Many questioned in response why accountability – by which I mean being answerable for a claim, able to describe what it rests on and respond when it’s challenged – should matter if verification has been solved. I suggested peer reviewers reserve their expert judgment for texts that don’t get flagged as heavily AI-written, so as to prioritize review as human exchange, but some see this as an obstruction to truth-seeking rather than an attempt to preserve it. The problem is that if we all agree that outputs matter–that we do care about the solutions to longstanding conjectures, that we do ultimately want to know how to cure diseases–then understanding appears as something separate. It’s cast as a mental state that looks optional next to the cure or the proof itself, and becomes easy to dismiss as a second-order constraint that we tack on because historically we’ve required it to arrive at the solutions in the first place. When defenders of understanding don’t dispute this separation, they immediately lose the argument. It becomes easy for the side that prioritizes output to peg them as simply not trying hard enough to envision a new future. But the superficial framing of understanding that we keep falling back on obscures deeper concerns that these examples share. They are less about anyone’s mental state than about what happens when something goes wrong. Tao’s scenario turns on the possibility that the AI passed the trial by exploiting a weakness in the trial itself. A paper whose authors can’t explain its claims leaves no one to consult if those claims fail. Where along the way did we come to believe that scientific value lies in correctness alone? This intuition is ultimately less about AI than it appears. The inclination to let AI drive science is less a sign of how forward-thinking one is about our future with AI, and more a symptom of a “value-free ideal” that has shaped our thinking since the Cold War era: a view that only epistemic criteria (not ethical and social values) deserve a place in judging what the evidence shows. That it pervades our debates about AI for science is not so surprising; it’s only in the last few decades or so that rejecting the value-free ideal became the philosophical mainstream. This ideal feeds unrealistic expectations and keeps us from seeing that pushback against the rapid infiltration of AI output into the scientific record is neither anti-AI nor anti-science. The stakes are bigger than any one debate or field. The value-free ideal distorts how we go about seeking truth, causing us to mistake verified results for knowledge. It threatens the human capacities that sustain science, causing us to see criticism and accountability as inconvenient overhead rather than the mechanics of knowledge production. It leaves us confused about what understanding is, and consequently why it matters. Subscribe Is science “naturally aligned”? The social contract for science represents an idealized relationship between science and society that arose after World War II in the US: scientists receive public funding and autonomy , and in return society receives the benefits of their inquiry. Built on a distinction between pure and applied science and a “linear model” in which basic research feeds applied work, the social contract replaces abstract arguments about the value of understanding with practical societal benefits, reshaping how we see science. Drawing on arguments made by concerned scientists in the late 1800s, who worried public celebration of new inventions like electric lights and the steam engine would crowd out respect for what they viewed as their more essential contributions, it also helped to forge a value-free ideal that says that at its core, science must be removed from “contextual values” like ethical or social concerns. For the social contract to gain broad societal buy-in as a model of scientific progress (and consequently shore up government investment in scientific research), we needed to imagine truth-seeking as the impersonal application of methods, immune to political or social pressures. Philosophers of science aspired to inquiry based only on “epistemic” (or “cognitive”) values. Any influence from the scientist’s intentions or values came to be seen as a risk that the right methods should minimize, laying the groundwork for today’s questions about why it should matter who asserted the claim so long as it’s correct. Many debates about AI’s role in science come down to disagreements about whether the scientific truth can be realized purely through use of the right procedures. Over the course of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there was almost a moralizing drive to eliminate as much of the scientist’s self as possible from the scientific process, so that trust in individuals could be replaced with trust in the system. AI agents set loose on the scientific literature, able to verify and intervene experimentally themselves, look like the long-awaited fulfillment of nineteenth century scientific ethics. Much of the “AI for science” rhetoric inherits what I call the “science is naturally aligned” premise: by enacting the scientific method at scale, with its various justification procedures, we can reach a place where we no longer need human judgment to produce truth. Is what is true really so separable from understanding or accountability? Math has become a centerpiece in recent debates because it gives us a case where correctness can be separated cleanly; a proof can be verified by AI without any human understanding how it works. What mathematicians still want after verification is a clue to what mechanical objectivity can’t provide. Truth as a value-driven practice Philosophers of science now predominantly reject the value-free ideal as being appropriate or helpful. Values enter because whether we reject or accept hypotheses is contingent on how we weigh consequences. Even in abstract realms like math, there are often simply too many possible truths for values not to be brought to bear in sifting through them. Mathematicians accepted long ago that in principle a machine can enumerate the set of theorems that can be proved from a given set of axioms. Yet the scale of this space is immense, motivating people to seek clever shortcuts for exploring it. But even with automated theorem-proving at scale, not all theorems are equally interesting to people. Values are inherent in the choices that lead to certain open problems gaining widespread appeal, and in the processes by which the community comes to accept and internalize the results. Fermat’s Last Theorem initially got attention not because it was an inherently important conjecture, but because Fermat claimed to have a proof but never provided it, enticing others to try their hand. It became central when it was shown that it would follow from the modularity conjecture, which proposed a previously unanticipated link between disparate areas of math. It was considered solved after peer review exposed an error that led to a corrected version of the original proof, even though formal verification didn’t come until recently. Epistemic taste develops because without it, we face an undifferentiated flood of facts. Taste is a capacity we develop over time as we choose problems, pursue some of them, and see which yield new understanding or ideas. If AI takes over choosing, we risk losing the personal fulfillment and community cooperation that motivates many to want to develop a capacity for scientific judgment in the first place. Tao makes a similar point by framing open problems as lighthouses rather than destinations. Reaching them prematurely with AI may sterilize the field around them. If, as fields are transformed by AI, we stop producing people who can judge what’s interesting and aligned with human aspirations, we may end up with a science that fails to serve basic human interests. Its results will consume attention from those to whom it is targeted, while providing neither fodder for subsequent discoveries nor contributing to the processes that help shape the next generation. This starts to sound like motivation for a new kind of linear model for science, which ensures that human reflection and inquiry are sustained despite AI becoming better than the average mathematician. The risk of proceeding without human intervention is drift, as anyone who relies heavily on agents to carry out their work knows. Even when you think you’re providing a well-specified pipeline for implementing and verifying an idea, it’s easy to end up mired in nuance in some branch you never expected to traverse. When you don’t assert epistemic agency, you can easily end up with a “view from nowhere” – not a form of pure objectivity, but an answer without a corresponding question. Maintaining alignment is not a problem you solve once and move on from. It requires a supply of humans who can articulate and adjudicate between values. Mechanical objectivity attempted to replace trust in individuals with trust in procedures, but that substitution has never happened as intended. To understand why, we need to look at the interactions that truth-seeking depends on. Sociality is not contamination of rationality There’s a tendency to see the social aspects of science as opposed to rationality. The social side of science can produce pathologies, like bad conventions, herd behavior, or deference to prestige. But scientific knowledge as we know it has always been the product of many epistemic agents bringing values and expertise to bear, and revising their views in response to challenge, not from some external verifying engine. As the philosopher Helen Longino argues , the basis for objective public knowledge is a shared language and a belief that things we describe exist independently of how we perceive them. If we can agree on descriptions of the world, then two things become possible: we can defer to others’ experiences to obtain knowledge, and meaningfully criticize scientific claims. Scientific communities develop shared standards and vocabulary that allow us to build on one another’s findings. We don’t need to verify everything firsthand, and sometimes relying on others’ findings can give us better grounds for believing something than investigating it ourselves, particularly when they possess evidence or expertise that we lack. Without criticism, we cannot have objectivity; it is, as Longino puts it “dependent upon the depth and scope of the transformative interrogation that occurs in any given scientific community.” For criticism to be transformative requires someone who is obliged to take it up. Practices like peer review and post-publication critique are not just fact-checks for sifting out false positives – they are about members of the community holding one another to the commitments that their assertions imply, and negotiating where to draw the line on the influence of personal preference. As Longino explains, “[t]he function of peer review is not just to check that the data seem right and the conclusions well-reasoned, but to bring to bear another point of view on the phenomena, whose expression might lead the original author(s) to revise the way they think about and present their observations and conclusions.” Method itself is best understood as a social process, where progress depends on how well a community sustains critical dialogue. This dialogue builds the people in it, shaping what it means for them to understand and exercise judgment along with the knowledge it produces. If criticism and an ability to trust others’ assertions are integral to the production of knowledge, we might ask whether AI can fulfill these same functions. Can models realize transformative criticism without human involvement? Can we trust the assertions of AI agents without obtaining direct understanding ourselves? And if we do, what happens to our own capacity to question, criticize, and stand behind results? What does it mean to assert something is true? The view that it shouldn’t matter who asserted some result as long as it’s correct corresponds to reliabilist epistemologies in philosophy. Classical epistemology insisted that true beliefs are only knowledge if the believer is able to produce reasons for their belief. In contrast, reliabilist epistemologies argue that true beliefs can, at least in some cases, represent genuine knowledge even when the believer can’t produce justifying reasons, provided they arrived at those beliefs by exercising capacities that are reliable producers of true beliefs in those circumstances. But there are limits to what reliability can provide. The philosopher Robert Brandom imagines a community where the members hold true beliefs, which they have acquired through reliable means, but cannot offer reasons for any of them. Because attributing reliability to the source of their beliefs would itself provide a form of justification based on inference, the community can’t know that they are reliable. They are reliable as instruments indicating something about their surroundings, but unable to recognize themselves as such. Unable to even possess the concept of reliability, Brandom concludes, they cannot have knowledge. If reliability alone can’t produce knowledge, what can? Brandom’s response is that calling something knowledge is a social act. To call what someone has “knowledge,” we have to attribute to them a commitment (that they believe that thing) along with an entitlement to that belief (that it is justified). But we also have to undertake that commitment ourselves, in the sense that we endorse the belief. The scientist who first asserted the claim allows us to repeat the claim (and draw conclusions from it) while leaving them responsible for justifying it if challenged. We do this relatively easily in human science because if it turns out there was something wrong with the original assertion, there is an answerable source we can consult to resolve it. Assertions have social significance because we can hold the original author accountable for what was said. This is the sense of understanding that matters most for science, that mathematicians want after the proof has been verified, and that Tao’s patient wants too: results that can be interrogated and reconceptualized where needed, to avoid the perception of progress that fails to serve our goals. But when we rely on AI results we don’t understand, there is only the person whose name is on the result to turn to. This is the problem arXiv is concerned with: no author can take responsibility for what they cannot understand, and hence they cannot respond to criticism by saying what it rests on, or whether it should be withdrawn. In other words, formal authorship survives while substantive authorship weakens . And so we lose the potential for transformative criticism, which is what sustains our notions of “objective” results in the first place. Could AI act as an accountable epistemic agent? A natural question is whether we could put the criticism to the AI agent itself, letting it decide whether to defend the result or concede and revise. What would it mean for AI to be an epistemic agent capable of committing to its assertions? There are a few challenges with today’s agents that would need to be overcome. One is their lack of persistence and identity in the sense that we attribute it to people. An agent that retracts something it asserted in one session is not bound to maintain its correction or the reasoning behind it in the next. If each new result is produced by a new bespoke multi-agent infrastructure, it becomes hard to “keep score” in the way that naturally happens within networks of human scientists. Scientific knowledge production depends on epistemic agents who have something at stake. Making bad claims changes the scientist’s standing in the community, which is how trust in individuals can remain calibrated. It’s not clear what comparable loss an AI agent faces in retracting its assertions, particularly given its lack of persistence. To overcome such limitations would require a considerable shift in how we develop AI: away from being maximally helpful in each exchange and toward being accountable across them, as human scientists tend to be. This may well be possible. But I don’t think accountable AI will be enough to sustain meaningful science from our human perspective. Let’s say we succeed in developing agents that can answer for claims. This is half of what accountability demands, but we also need others capable of holding them accountable, by asking for evidence, questioning assumptions, recognizing when an answer is evasive. Endorsements of others’ assertions are only as good as our capacity to engage with what we are endorsing. These are capacities that get built by exercising them, by choosing problems, defending our work, reviewing papers, challenging others’ results. When we don’t exercise our capacities, we lose them. It’s not clear what we gain from a perfectly accountable AI if no one can judge how good its answers are. We’d have truth-seeking in theory, but no one who is able to do it. Thurston’s notion of mathematical success points to this shared capacity to interrogate, extend, and repair a field’s knowledge that he’s hinting at. As he puts it, “As long as people in the field are comfortable that the idea works, it doesn’t need to have a formal written source.” Verification can tell us a result checks out in a technical sense, but only a community of people prepared to stand behind it can turn it into knowledge. If we continue to appeal to value-free ideals that frame correctness as all that matters, we will keep building tools that prioritize answers while neglecting the truth-seeking and understanding of the people who can make them count. Cosmos Institute is the Academy for Philosopher-Builders, technologists building AI for human flourishing. We run fellowships, fund fast prototypes, and host seminars with institutions like Oxford, Aspen Institute, and Liberty Fund. Subscribe 52 6 14 Share Previous Next Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Daniel Dal Monte 5d Liked by Jessica Hullman Powerful article! Reply Share JEFF TSAO 5h Liked by Jessica Hullman Verification vs knowledge reminds me of the distinction engineers draw between verification and validation. Verification asks whether we built the product right, meaning whether it meets its specification. Validation asks whether we built the right product, meaning whether it actually serves the people it’s meant to serve. AI can be extraordinarily good at verification--checking a result against a well-posed specification. Validation is harder, because it requires an intimate understanding of the human user: what they need, what they value. There's knowledge in both verification and validation, but verification lives more on the "is this a good answer" side while validation lives more on the "is this a good question" side. title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
body_text: Stringman from Neufangled Robotics Store Docs Playroom My Robots Future Room-scale cable robot Open source and air gappable $795 Add to cart Tech specs Your browser does not support the video tag. ≥ 0.5 kg ≥ 1.0 kg ≥ 1.5 kg ≥ 2.0 kg Payload capacity at the 28 N line tension limit, net of the 638 g gripper, in a 7 × 7 × 3 m room, anchors in the ceiling corners. Explore your own room → Tension is all you need In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly. Name Actuator count Average payload over work volume Stringman 4 1.9 kg Typical arm * 7 0.32 kg * 0.75 m serial arm using the same DM-H6215 1 N·m direct drive actuators at rated torque, ignoring the weight of its own links. Stringman figure is for a 7 × 7 × 3 m room at the 28 N line tension limit, net of its 638 g gripper and marker. Technical Specs Work area Room sizes between 3m and 10m (XY diagonal). Room heights between 2.3m and 4m Payload Up to 2.2 kg near the floor, 1.9 kg on average. Traverse speed ~0.4 m/s Cameras 2 anchor cameras @ 1920x1080 30fps and 1 wide FOV gripper camera @ 684x384 60fps Compute External. (Your PC as controller) Raspberry Pi Zero 2W (gripper) and Pi 3A+ (anchors). Connectivity 5 GHz Wi-Fi using QR-codes for simple setup. (gripper 2.4 Ghz only) Materials 3D printed. Structural parts: PET-GF, Decorative parts: PLA Mounting options Wooden stud backed drywall or plaster wall mounts. Strapping to structural columns. Endurance ~1000h of testing in real homes accumulated so far. Open, and Under Your Control Stringman is open source and OSHWA certified . The mechanical CAD, the PCBs , and the control software are all published. We believe owners should be in control of their own robots. That's why Stringman can run air gapped on your local Wi-Fi network: the UI is served locally, AI models run on your own hardware, and no data ever leaves your network. STL files 4 DM-H6215 $66 2 STS3215 $21 2 RasPi 3A+ $25 1 RasPi Zero 2W $18 … Bill of materials Build guide # calculate line data from motor data self .last_length = self .sc.get_unspooled_length( self .last_angle) self .meters_per_rev = self .sc.get_unspool_rate( self .last_angle) current_line_speed = (motor_vel / twopi) * self .meters_per_rev self .last_tension = (-(smooth_torque - self .direction * hold) * twopi) / self .meters_per_rev Code so the feature-section alternation is unchanged. --> The Courier for Your Home Lab Give your home lab the capability of carrying parts from one workcell to another anywhere in the room, so you can get more out of your other robots. The Python API and MCP server is made for agents so you can get your workflow running right away. 2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RSR model by No Limits , CC BY 4.0 , simplified. SO-101 arm from TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100 , Apache 2.0. Unmatched Reach Unlike desktop arms limited to a fixed radius, Stringman leverages a cable-driven architecture to access the full volume of a room. The work area volume per dollar of this type of robot is completely unmatched, all with fewer actuators than even the simplest mobile robots. Anchors and eylets are mounted in the corners of the room near the ceiling and define a four-sided work area within which any object can be moved from point to point. Stringman Research arm Work area 7 × 7 × 3 m room (147 m³) 0.75 m hemisphere (0.88 m³) Price $795 $2,500 Volume per $1,000 185 m³ 0.35 m³ That's roughly 500× the work area volume per dollar, at comparable 2 kg payload. What do I need to install Stringman? A room where you can secure the anchors to studs or columns. A computer to run the controller with some NPU or GPU (macs work great!) A handheld drill A step ladder that lets you reach the ceiling. 1 Secure the cleats 2 Hang the anchors 3 Run calibration Secure the cleats to wall studs near the ceiling with wood screws, or to columns with ratchet straps. Hang the anchors and connect the lines to the gripper. Run calibration. This hands off process takes about five minutes and adapts Stringman to your room. Step-by-step: picture guide or video guide Have a ceiling fan? That's fine. The original prototype was built in a room with a ceiling fan, and it still runs there today. Mount the anchors at or below the level of the blades and the lines can't physically reach it. Training new models Several methods are available for control with default models for automatic grasping, target, and destination selection to make it easy to quickly build new behaviors. Stringman is fully capable of LeRobot control using including Pi.05, JEPA, Multitask DiT, and others. Collecting training data for new behaviors can be done from the UI, and as few as 50 episodes can be enough for certain models like DiT to learn a behavior. Move across the video to scrub Gripper camera · naavox/bedroom-oct15 , episode 0 0.00 s Frequently Asked Questions Will there be lines crossing my room? As long as it remains installed, yes. However, when parked, they are up near the ceiling and out of the way. Clutter on the ceiling is preferable to clutter on the floor in our opinion. If you need to remove the anchors, they can be detached from their mounts without tools, leaving a relatively small white cleat on the wall. Can it be used in rooms with ceiling fans? Yes, it's just a matter of mounting the anchors at or below the level of the fan, making it physically impossible for the lines or marker tag to touch it. Similarly, the work area can be shrunk to exclude low hanging light fixtures if they are off to the side, but if the center of the room does contain low hanging objects, Stringman cannot be installed in that room. What happens if someone is caught in the wires? When reaching a tension limit of 28 newtons (about the weight of a backpack), all motors relax and the lines can be pulled loose. Since they are overhead most of the time, it's uncommon for people to collide with them. Can it be controlled remotely? Not by default, but if you bind it with neufangled.com/playroom then you or anyone you share access with can operate it from anywhere, and access can be revoked at any time. Neufangled Robotics does not store any of the information from your robot that is forwarded through its servers. Remote Management For those who prefer to make the trade-off by binding their robot to an account, our web-based console allows you to monitor and control Stringman from anywhere. Think of it as a security camera with a hand. If you do decide that you would like to make use of our cloud telemetry relay, You can use it, and still go back to a completely lan only mode whenever you want. Your data is never collected. Set Your Drop Bins Organizing your home is a physical process, not a coding task. Use our clip-on fiducial tags to designate your laundry bin, toy box, and trash can. Stringman maps these locations visually. You don't need to tag individual pieces of clutter—just the destination. If there's something you never want it to pick up, you can mark that item as off-limits. Networks trained to control stringman have learned that the word "toybox" refers to that tag, so you can use it to mark anything even if it doesn't look like the toyboxes from our training set. You can also use the tags as arbitrary source and destination markers for ferry jobs, such as carrying items from one robot arm to another. or carrying laundry from the ground to a robotic folding station For Educators A classroom with a Stringman robot gives your students a chance to become familiar with robotics fundamentals such as inverse kinematics, telemetry, and imitation learning while controlling an exotic and capable flying gripper. If you have walls and a MacBook, you're more than halfway there. Cross embodiment is one of the biggest challenges in robotics, and showing that a model can operate a vastly different body type is a stronger result than moving it from one bimanual robot to another. Our datasets are public on Hugging Face , there's a controller-in-the-loop MuJoCo sim, and Stringman works with LeRobot, making it one of the most inexpensive robots to test on and a natural capstone project. No Charging Downtime Mobile robots spend a significant portion of their time charging. Because Stringman is a powered from the wall, it's always ready for work. Furthermore, by removing the heavy battery pack, we've increased the payload capacity per dollar compared to mobile platforms that must waste energy carrying their own power supply. The gripper's power is delivered via one of the support cables. A two-conductor FEP jacketed twisted pair cable with a tensile strength of 50N. Swing Cancellation What's that pole for? Stringman's gripper hangs below the pivot point so it can reach the floor next to beds and tables. This additional linkage could allow unconstrained motion so Stringman employs active swing cancellation algorithms to counteract momentum, without adding the cost of any additional motors. This ensures the gripper remains steady and predictable even during rapid cross-room traversals. There's a whole video about swing cancellation if you're curious about how it works! Wrist and Fingers Often, a simple solution that gets the job done has more value than a complex one. Stringman uses a two fingered gripper with a wrist. This is enough dexterity for the clutter it is designed to pick up, keeping weight and cost low and reliability high. In our household tests we have determined that more layers of grip tape is simply a better return on investment than more articulated fingers. The gripper can rotate it's wrist to better place the fingers around flat sided or long objects. Blends In Like the fishing line, the anchors themselves are not trying to be seen. The cover can be painted or re-printed to match your room. Customize Your Look The Stringman faceplate is easily swappable. Grab the STL or bambu 3MF files to print your faceplate in any color. Join Server Mailing List Subscribe for major product announcements, software updates, and new hardware releases. Subscribe YouTube Watch full demonstrations, tutorials, and deep-dives into Stringman's kinematics and build processes. title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
body_text: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time | nns.ee Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time Nov 02, 2026 Permalink: https://blog.nns.ee/2026/11/02/renault-hack/ The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain. When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it. They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there. Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it. I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much. Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there. That never happened. The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it. I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious . Just RE it Still in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu. Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit ( https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md ). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves. When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont ) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10. After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet. This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me. What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps. I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time. I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying. Fine . I'll just root it and do it myself. Easy wins? I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root. I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins. My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it. While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected. It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls. I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing. Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could. Back to the drawing board I'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved. For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system: rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro) Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard , and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi , which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal , which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec . This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011. Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script , a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time. I reversed ttn , the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed. More wild goose chases I still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector. As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input. I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX / SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver , which launched whatever command line was provided with execve . This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh , which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec . The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful. Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage. Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt ) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root. It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system. However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end. Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes. Borrowing a trick from kernel exploits I had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together. Among other things, I knew I could: Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfs Write ASCII to paths of my own choosing This is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead? Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead ( |/bin/my-coredump-handler ). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there. core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28. Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern . I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh . This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root. Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script. I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect. Putting it together My final master.script turned out to be quite simple: #define LOGFILE .. / .. / proc / sys / kernel / core_pattern LOG |/ bin / sh / media / sdcard / payload.sh SHEX / bin / dbus - monitor I initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the " Execute master.script? " prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution. The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd . With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat , which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn't really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180. I changed it to 120. That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.
