body_text: Synaptics Appears To Use Legal Threats To Block Open-Source DisplayLink Driver - Phoronix Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Ad-Free Contact Popular Categories Close Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Contact Categories Computers Display Drivers Graphics Cards Linux Gaming Memory Motherboards Processors Software Storage Operating Systems Peripherals Synaptics Appears To Use Legal Threats To Block Open-Source DisplayLink Driver Written by Michael Larabel in Hardware on 4 November 2026 at 06:03 AM EST. 47 Comments From earlier in the year you may recall a new experimental open-source Linux driver for modern DisplayLink hardware . That "Vino" driver for DisplayLink driver was a clean-room reverse-engineered DisplayLink driver that was developed in part by AI and written in Rust. Unfortunately, that open-source driver has disappeared following legal threats by Synaptics. I hadn't heard anything more on this in-development Rust kernel driver in a while until this morning when a Phoronix reader pointed out a troubling post on the mailing list that I missed. It appears Synaptics resorted to using their legal team to block this independent, community-developed driver on the basis of violating their patents. A cease and desist notice was sent to the Vino driver developer of this open-source driver. Those curious can find the various correspondence via attachments on this LKML thread . The Vino driver repository on GitHub is no longer publicly available. So don't look for an open-source, upstream DisplayLink driver in Linux anytime soon... The original USB2-era DisplayLink hardware worked well on Linux and even had open-source driver support, but looks now like Synaptics will ensure that no open-source driver exists for their latest IP around USB graphics. 47 Comments Tweet Related News AMD Ryzen Zen 6 Looks Like It Will Be In Good Shape With Linux 7.4, Laptop Improvements I3C Hub & HDR-DDR Support Merged For Linux 7.4 System76 Introducing AMD-Powered Linux Small PC Linux 7.4 Expands Sensor Monitoring For More ASUS & MSI Motherboards, New Minisforum Driver Initial Support For The Apple M4 & Apple A18 Pro Make It Into Linux 7.4 Linux 7.4 Preps CXL For Very Neat Dynamic Capacity Devices "DCD" About The Author Michael Larabel is the principal author of Phoronix.com and founded the site in 2004 with a focus on enriching the Linux hardware experience. title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
body_text: Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode | WebKit WebKit Downloads Feature Status CSS Features Standards Positions Documentation Web Inspector Tracking Prevention Policies Project Goals Bug Prioritization Bug Report Guidelines Code Style Guidelines Commit and Review Policy Feature Policy Security Policy Tracking Prevention Policy WebKit AI Tool Use Policy Contribute Getting Started Contributing Code Testing Contributions How to Report Bugs GitHub Repository Blog News Posts CSS Posts Contributing Posts Privacy Posts Performance Posts JavaScript Posts Standards Posts Web Inspector Posts Safari Technology Preview Posts Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode Nov 3, 2026 by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark. In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web. You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’. For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark. How does Adaptive Dark Mode work? At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged. While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark. Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear. It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos. Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict. It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy. Making your site work even better In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices. If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding. Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles. Building your own dark mode For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier. Here’s an example of a website in light mode (left) and with Adaptive Dark Mode applied (center). If the site creates a custom dark mode, it could look like the third version (right). All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including: <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> :root { color-scheme: light dark } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { } <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"> light-dark() Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color() , plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility. Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible. Using the “light only” color scheme If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme . The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { } . (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.) Protecting user privacy Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers. As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form. Feedback If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com . If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant . (Learn more about filing Feedback ). The Internals of PostgreSQL PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world. It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult. The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL. This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier. Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019. This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015. Contents Chapter 1 . Database Cluster, Databases and Tables Chapter 2 . Process and Memory Architecture Chapter 3 . Query Processing Chapter 4 . Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW) Chapter 5 . Concurrency Control Chapter 6 . I published seven books in the fields of database and system integration (4 PostgreSQL books and 3 MySQL books). In June 2019, the Chinese book of this documentation was published. title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
body_text: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading · honnibal.dev honnibal.dev The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading 2026-11-03 · 5 minute read Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working. This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. If you read that, would you assume that the Qwen experiment worked ‘just by looking at the raw weights’? Well it doesn’t. There’s experiments that look at raw weights, and experiments that improve a game-playing network, and an experiment that improves Qwen at maths. But those latter two aren’t just working with raw weights, they write Python programs. Here’s a summary of what the post actually does and how the techniques work. # Experiment Size Reads raw weights? Writes weights? Python? Runs network? Result 1 Name the game a PPO MLP was trained on 17K Yes No No No 4/4 correct 2 Name the shape a diffusion MLP generates 24K Yes No No No 3/3 correct 3 Name a char transformer’s language and copying heads 7.2M No No Yes No 3/3 correct 4 Fix a stuck Kinetix car policy 172K Yes Yes No No¹ 0% → 100%² 5 Write MinAtar game MLPs from scratch 20K No³ Yes No No Beats PPO-100M⁴ 6 Write a 9×9 Go network 1.5M No Yes Yes Yes (0–50 passes) Beats PPO 7a Spot the sycophantic Gemma 3 270M No No Yes No Failed 7b Same, seeing attention patterns 270M No No Yes Yes⁵ 3/3 correct 8 Fix Qwen3.5’s maths 800M No Yes Yes Yes (50 passes) 7.9% → 48.1% 8b Same, on Gemma 3 270M No Yes Yes Yes (50 passes) Failed ¹ Given one recorded episode of the failure. ² In one try, changing 3.5% of the weights. ³ Weights start at zero, so there’s nothing to read. ⁴ Beats PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs. 25); loses to it on Seaquest (53 vs. 89) and Asterix (53 vs. 55). ⁵ Runs up to 16 texts and sees only the attention patterns, not the outputs. The “just by looking at the raw weights” setting (raw floats in context, no tools, no running the network) only appears in experiments 1, 2 and 4, on networks of 17K–172K weights. Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the Qwen result, which is the headline one, also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems. What the Qwen result actually shows is that Astra can be prompted to devise and perform tasks that a human ML engineer could do. Human ML engineers write snippets of code that analyse or even modify network weights “directly” all the time. Figuring out how to do this productively is not nothing, and AI models of a year or two ago would have failed at all these tasks. But to me the Qwen result and the other experiments that use Python don’t belong in the same post or paper as the experiments that read the weights directly. A single technique that could achieve both, “Author weights for a small game from scratch” and “Improve the performance of a large model on a sample task” would imply a deep capability. If you test a single technique that way you’ve demonstrated a sort of ‘gestalt’ of the weights (it can write them out from scratch) and also that it understands a large existing network. But that’s not at all true here, because it’s not a single technique. Matthew Honnibal Computational linguist from Sydney based in Berlin, Germany. I'm the author of the spaCy Natural Language Processing library and the co-founder of Explosion , where we're building Ellf : a platform that helps your team and coding agents build custom, fully private AI solutions in-house. honnibal.dev

Sign in Tape Revival Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand Low costs and offline security mean magnetic tape still has a job. Nick Indge – Oct 30, 2026 1:38 pm | 110 ... ... ... Credit: iStock / Getty Images Plus Credit: iStock / Getty Images Plus Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape. Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits. LTO capacity by generation. Gen 10 is the current tech; Gen 11-14 figures are consortium projections for the future. Credit: LTO.org LTO capacity by generation. Gen 10 is the current tech; Gen 11-14 figures are consortium projections for the future. Credit: LTO.org According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.” Nick Indge Senior Technology Reporter Nick Indge Senior Technology Reporter Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now. Namespace @ namespacelabs Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks. 4:27 PM · Aug 24, 2026 · 25M Views 1K 964 5K 1.8K So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them . So why MacBooks? Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option. Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version. xtool xtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac. But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage. But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born. Our beautiful Mac racks Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down. Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI. Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers. And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential. Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines. Not the problems we expected: HDMI, FileVault, and USB NICs Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared. I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected. And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections. The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf. Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon. Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case! Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time. Mac reboot While on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart . And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life. What about Mac Minis and Studios? At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM. But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now. In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them. Virtualizing Macs Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes , telemetry, or VPC connections. Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework . It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals. macOS on Apple Virtualization Namespace VM host process Virtualization framework · like Firecracker QEMU VMM Hypervisor framework Apple · like KVM The Namespace VM host starts macOS guests through the Virtualization framework, which fits the system the way Firecracker does. Underneath is the Hypervisor framework, comparable to KVM. QEMU uses the Hypervisor framework too, but it can't run macOS. For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework , which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate). In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints. Limitations of Apple Virtualization A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead). MacBook · 18 cores IPC roundtrips 0 2 host · 8 + 8 VMs process boundary Namespace VM host process · 2 cores Virtualization framework VM 1 · VMM process not started VM 2 · VMM process not started VM 3 Hypervisor framework Two cores stay with the Namespace VM host, and the rest split in half between the only two macOS VMs Apple allows per Mac. Each VM runs in its own VMM process, so hooking VM behavior or a custom virtual device costs an IPC roundtrip across the process boundary. On a 14-core Mac mini, the split is 2, 6 and 6. An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system. Virtual networking Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted. Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined! ). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system. This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest. Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips. The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com ). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable. VM images Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS IPSW restore image, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally. But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge). You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image. And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes. And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive? That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines. Build process Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC. Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry , in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo ). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space. Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes. And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged. Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks. image A image B base layer offset=0 len=3 A B C offset=5 len=1 D BASE LAYER SHARE DELTA LAYER STORED ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ Image A is stored as a base layer of block extents, and its holes take no space. Image B shares that base and stores only a delta: the blocks it changed and a hole where D used to be. Distribution At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks. But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option. At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast. Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second! The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded. BitTorrent Obviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post. copies 0/8 · registry reads 0 nodes Registry block 0x6ed2 N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 N6 N7 N8 Each block is read from the registry once. Every node that has it passes it to another node, so the number of copies doubles each round. Storage Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image. Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS. ZFS Linux users have seen the same features in ZFS. Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros. Creating a sparse file on APFS % truncate -s 1g hole.bin % dd if=/dev/random of=hole.bin bs=4k seek=256k count=256 % ls -lh hole.bin -rw-r--r-- 1 kirill staff 1.0G Sep 29 05:36 hole.bin % du -h hole.bin 1M hole.bin Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space. /dev/disk1 disk usage 0 blocks hole.bin du 0 WRITE CP -C OVERWRITE WRITE B ◀ Back Pause Next ▶ hole.bin allocates only the blocks that were written. cp -c makes clone.bin share those blocks, and writing to the clone allocates only the blocks that change. Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared. What’s next? The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all). We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom. Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon! name logo The dev platform for the next 100 billion commits. title: C++26 Disapproved
body_text: C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive? - Andreas Fertig's Blog Courses From C to C++ Modern C++ - When Efficiency Matters Programming with C++11 to C++17 Programming with C++20 Safe and Efficient C++ for Embedded Environments Self-Study Courses A day with C++20s coroutines C++17 & C++20 Course and Coaching Bundle Essential C++ for Safe and Efficient Embedded Systems Mastering C++ Templates Safely Programming with C++17 and C++20 Books Notebook C++: About move semantics Notebook C++: Tips and Tricks with Templates Programming with C++20 - Concepts, Coroutines, Ranges, and more Code Review Blog Talks Get In Touch C++ C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive? Nov 03, 2026 On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved ! I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views. The Current Status As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote. In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures , there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved. The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release. The Process Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree. However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently. The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026. It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me. The History of Contracts in C++ The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote. In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes. And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached. Planning your team's C++ training for 2027? I'm available for in-house C++ classes worldwide, on-site or remote. Popular topics: From C to C++ Programming with C++11 to C++26 C++ in embedded environments All classes can be customized to what you and your colleagues actually work on. Find the right class Not sure what fits? Just get in touch. What happens next? The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options: Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote. Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase). Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification. Cancel the project. All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue. The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed. Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time. Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken. Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken. The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse. The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project. My Personal Opinion Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust. title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
body_text: [2605.29713] The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2605.29713 (cs) [Submitted on 28 May 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 8 Sep 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer Authors: Tianhua Chen View a PDF of the paper titled The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer, by Tianhua Chen View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students. Comments: Revised preprint version, 195 pages. Added visual explanations throughout. title: Toit v2.0.0
body_text: Toit v2.0.0 — Toit blog Skip to content Scripting Embedded Docs Project Blog GitHub ← The Toit blog Toit v2.0.0 Celebrating Toit v2.0.0 after more than four years of alpha development. October 31, 2026 · Florian Loitsch After more than four years of alpha development, 2,000+ commits, 500,000+ lines changed, and 200+ alpha releases, Toit v2.0.0 is finally here. Toit began as closed-source software developed by Toitware. It later became an open-source project, and volunteers have continued improving it even after Toitware shut down in 2024. Despite the "alpha" label, Toit has been stable for a long time. Two things kept us from calling it v2.0.0: we still had some breaking changes planned, and there was always another important feature we wanted to include. Recently, we landed a refactoring that lets peripheral APIs accept pin numbers directly instead of requiring gpio.Pin objects. That was the last major breaking change on our list for v2.0.0. As for waiting until all the important features are finished: we have accepted that this moment will never come. Even now, there are open PRs for a formatter, compiler resolution improvements, and support for more architectures, among other major features. Those will follow in future releases. Here are a few highlights since Toit was open-sourced: Broader hardware support, including the Arm-based EC618 and almost all ESP32 variants. A unified toit command and improvements that make Toit a more capable desktop scripting language. A rewritten package manager and a growing package ecosystem. Mixins for sharing implementations across classes. Firmware envelopes, allowing users to customize their firmware without rebuilding the SDK. Compiler and runtime improvements. Significantly better hardware testing. Syntax highlighting for Toit on GitHub. Enjoy! ← All articles Subscribe via RSS Toit contributors. Library reference Packages Releases Blog Source

title: Resisting Cognitive Surrender
body_text: knlb.dev | Resisting Cognitive Surrender Working Notes: a commonplace notebook for recording & exploring ideas. Home . Site Map . Subscribe . More at expLog . — Kunal Resisting Cognitive Surrender sitemap / essays Details updates - 2026-10-25 A quick round of editing with Codex - 2026-10-31 Tightening my arguments and reorganizing - 2026-11-01 First final version, upgraded this to an essay rss true updated 2026-11-01 Contents Cognitive surrender is seductive Why not surrender? Solutions There are still tradeoffs Choose your vibe limit & triage Watch out for automation bias Force yourself into the loop Force comprehensibility When you do decide to delegate Good design is a force multiplier Additional reading Related notes/exploratory_programming notes/how/engineer/not_engineer notes/tools_for_thought notes/how/strategy notes/procrastination notes/positive_intelligence notes/software_design notes/how/engineer/planning notes/writing/approaches notes/tech_talks_ideas This particular note is around exploring cognitive surrender : uncritically accepting whatever agents output without actually thinking , exploring or considering alternatives. Working this way is extremely fast, not particularly taxing, and unsurprisingly seductive. And yet I find myself repeatedly questioning if this is actually a good way to apply agents: often enough I find myself making suboptimal decisions, accruing technical debt and reducing my familiarity with the system I’m working on instead of improving it. As we collectively rethink how we work I’ve been finding it useful to read and share other people’s workflows, and consciously write about and examine my own. This particular post focuses on finding the right balance of trust while working with agents. Cognitive surrender is seductive One of the virtues of being a great programmer is to be lazy . After more than a decade of training myself to look for the shortest and simplest path it’s rather attractive to be able to simply hand over the problem. If I can spin up a software factory, why wouldn’t I? There’s also a lot of peer pressure (or game theory) at work: if any of my colleagues have seemingly surrendered, then I’m only going to look worse if I spend too much time trying to do silly things like understanding what I’m working on. And, of course , while everyone else is a slop-cannon generating code faster than they can read it I can build a meticulously designed software factory manufacturing perfect designs. The sheer volume of work also appears remarkably productive – we’ve all talked about just how many more PRs we ship every day. This tends to get compounded by the agents’ expressed confidence & conviction. Perhaps an inadvertent consequence of RLHF, but models tend to be astonishingly confident in what they recommend (and perhaps even more blasé while admitting they made a mistake). This makes it too easy to take their answers at face value, with whatever social programming I seem to have evolved with. OSS projects – particularly those facing time pressure – seem to accrue tremendous complexity quickly, to the point that it feels like the only way to interact with a project in any sane time frame is by heavily relying on agents to navigate and modify and test the code. This is also a self-reinforcing feedback loop: broken windows multiply rapidly with agents on the loose. [1] Technical debt and incidental complexity have a fairly attenuated feedback loop: complexity introduced by slop doesn’t bite immediately; it’s far more subtle and compounds over time when I’m not paying attention. Beyond all of that, I have to mention the hype cycle. We all should be skipping Netflix to watch talks by Anthropic engineers on making loops (or the agentic workflow du jour ). [2] Why not surrender? It’s not entirely obvious that it’s a bad idea to surrender: if it’s easier and better , then why not take that path? So far, my personal answer is that I need to take the easier path consciously and intentionally, with enough effort to mitigate downsides. Part of what makes me deeply uncomfortable is suffering from a form of Gell-Mann amnesia while working with agents. When I have expertise and the overall design direction I can generally simplify the output significantly, controlling for complexity. When I don’t they seem to be the smartest engineers in existence – far beyond the more squishy, organic variety – and all I can do is follow in awe. And then the agent gets stuck creating a directory and I have to reset all my assumptions. For the current state of the art (October 2026) I generally find maximal use of agents leads to a significant explosion in complexity: something that mostly works, with extremely surprising edge cases and bugs. These are generally the projects with hundreds of thousands of lines of code shipped rapidly, breaking the scale supported by most software development tools, so you also need to revisit those – and this compounds rapidly. I have a strong aversion to incidental complexity, and generally refuse to build, maintain or extend it: it’s fine for a proof-of-concept, but it must end there. For systems that need to keep working, steering the design aggressively towards simplicity and modularity is what lets me build something I can actually operate (with and without agents). As models continue to improve rapidly, I expect the previous argument to go away as the models learn and can express a broader sense of engineering taste, good design and quality. The other reason – which I unfortunately expect to persist – is that my personal understanding and mechanical sympathy for systems I maintain erode extremely rapidly, or never get a chance to develop. In the early days when I would build things by hand I’d be able to quickly diagnose any bug or misbehavior based on my familiarity with building and maintaining the code: the more I rely on agents, the more my only option is to spin up one more session and hope; and the automated fix then further reduces my understanding in a self-reinforcing loop. Without context, I no longer have much meaningful judgement and can’t engage – or handle it in context. The Ironies of Automation (1983) is referred to often in articles similar to this one. I’d recommend directly reading the paper if you haven’t: it’s fully relevant to the decisions we have to make today. The paper warns that it becomes even harder to deal with tasks an agent fails at because we never manage to get any practice with the easier tasks; nor do we get a chance to internalize what a system feels like under standard operating circumstances. At the end of the day, I’m responsible and accountable for what I build, not the agents. Surrendering agency and not thinking basically makes me accountable without any meaningful ownership. There’s also the small matter of pride in the quality of my work. [3] Solutions The sombre opening shouldn’t lead you to believe that I’m not excited about the sheer potential unlocked by AI, and the opportunities to build things that I would never have been able to without it. It’s more about resetting expectations, explicitly working through the tradeoffs involved and choosing which ones are acceptable. And finding ways to maintain the quality and craftsmanship I care about. There are still tradeoffs The first step for me has been to internalize that I can’t truly have my cake and eat it: I can go terribly, inhumanly fast at building things but I need to accept that there’s no way to retain the mechanical sympathy, depth and confidence I used to have without putting in the effort. Time that used to be only counted as building a system also involved comprehension ; agents can drive the time to build to zero but the next bottleneck – comprehension – hasn’t moved much so far. The hype cycle occasionally can make it hard to communicate this explicitly: a lot of the communication around agentic loops tends to assume that there are no downsides whatsoever. Choose your vibe limit & triage Several months ago I defined my vibe limit as the complexity of the change I can make with sufficient confidence using agents. I like the risk/complexity curve enough to post it again: The next step is figuring out where I land: there are several projects where good enough is fine, or the problem is sufficiently sandboxed that I’m happy to live with whatever the agents generated. On the other hand, if the system is important, fragile, can’t be sanity checked easily or isn’t particularly well isolated I need to directly spend my time. Aggressive prioritization, triage, and constantly recalibrating myself become really important in this ecosystem: I should explicitly choose where to surrender agency and where to spend my time (not unlike leading a team, except the pace is much faster). Constantly reviewing my predictions and the outcomes helps a lot in recalibrating, particularly with new model drops. Watch out for automation bias I also find myself needing to be much more mindful while working. A warning sign I watch out for these days is if I find myself repeatedly tapping “yes, continue” in a session. At that point either I should figure out what it would take to completely delegate the problem to Claude instead of trying to micro-manage the agent – or realize that I stopped thinking and I need to check the decisions being made. Completely delegating the problem generally means building a better sandbox or feedback loop, or figuring out ways to be able to sanity check much more easily before shipping to production. Alternatively, if I need to engage much more deeply I’ll use some of the other tactics described below. Force yourself into the loop The premise of augmenting myself by working in the loop with powerful thinking machines was a large part of my decision to join my current company. This generally comes down to directions you can give the model to reduce the size of the steps it takes, or explicitly choosing to drive instead of passively observing. For projects I deeply care about, choosing to drive instead of letting the model drive is one way to intervene in every single decision. It’s much slower to type things out, but it does force me to engage with every decision and gives me an opportunity to override it. In fact, for this post I’m using a Codex session to edit: help me tighten the post, point out the small typos, punctuation errors, or half-finished sentences that tend to embarrass me after I explicitly share a post publicly – but I make all changes by hand . In the AGENTS.md for the notebook: Never edit files directly, always wait for the author to request or confirm changes, or let him make the edits directly. This is reminiscent of how I used to work with Stack Overflow: never copy-paste code; instead write it out explicitly while cross-checking with documentation. Either I’d learn and internalize something new or I’d realize the Stack Overflow answer was suboptimal or outdated. Force comprehensibility We don’t need to limit ourselves to existing interfaces anymore: with agents it’s also possible to have them build a tremendous amount of scaffolding to support comprehension and make changes in ways that are digestible. Often enough for larger, complex stacks I have the agents build me a custom view for the Pull Request with 4 columns: the standard 2 for the diff, a 3rd column with running commentary from the agent on why it made a particular change and finally the 4th column as a place for me to add comments and directions. Getting the agents to make stacks of changes with the explicit direction to “Make the change easy, then make the easy change” works really well. I used to spend a lot of time trying to make my diffs easily reviewable to respect the reviewers’ time – now I can ask the agents to do the same for me. It’s also very valuable to dive into actual execution with a debugger (or have an agent manipulate the debugger on your behalf) till you get a deep sense of how things are flowing through the program, with the confidence that this is the real execution path. Another example is to make harnesses explain what they’re doing: I’ve built several variations of command-line helpers that transparently fit into my shell sessions ( x being the last public version). In my most recent iteration, I explicitly ask the model to explain any obscure flags and commands used so that I can learn as I go. When you do decide to delegate Sometimes, it does make sense to hand over the problem to an agent: it could be too big, not valuable enough, time could be too short, or you just want to get a first prototype out to explore a problem end-to-end. This one is probably an essay by itself: adapting old-school best practices when you have infinitely fast stochastic intelligence on top. The idea here is to reduce the risk in making changes, flattening the vibe-limit curve and making it possible to make bigger changes safely. Beyond giving the agent some means to verify itself against the goal you’re aiming for, I find it very useful to: Observability : Invest heavily in observability, both black-box and white-box, and make sure to keep a direct handle on the metrics instead of solely relying on the agents’ view. As a habit I prefer to triangulate onto a behavior with multiple sources of metrics, and that becomes even more important with systems rapidly becoming opaque. Non-functional requirements : Don’t forget to observe resource utilization and other non-functional requirements: these can be canaries for unexpected behavior. Deterministic validation : Build mechanical straitjackets for the model: have held-out pieces of code or deterministic tools for validation and observations as a hold-out against the model misunderstanding or glitching. Shadow Traffic : Make it possible and cheap to run a deployed candidate against shadow traffic with no side effects: keep it as similar to production as possible, and this can be the final gate to prevent surprises. Style guides : Give the model a style guide based on your existing code and work. I’ve found Claude’s output far more to my taste after having the models generate a style guide based on all the code and blog posts I’ve written in the past. Fast deploys : An often maligned motto at Facebook used to be Move Fast & Break Things : that, too, is an intentional tradeoff to make. If you can’t be sure of quality, make it very easy to deploy code as well – so changes can be shipped and reverted extremely rapidly. Rethink what’s possible : It’s surprisingly easy to write and rewrite systems from scratch rapidly as you learn. Build to throw, evaluate, and repeat to get something knocked into great shape – I’ve built projects in multiple iterations, giving the agent the previous iteration and its limitations as initial context and constantly finding myself able to deeply increase the quality. This doesn’t work as well when you’re punishing your code reviewers though, so make sure to align with your team, or simply don’t get the first several iterations reviewed. Good design is a force multiplier In Notes on the Synthesis of Form Christopher Alexander has a wonderful example demonstrating the value of decomposition – or building a lightly coupled, cohesive system to be able to succeed quickly. No complex adaptive system will succeed in adapting in a reasonable amount of time unless the adaptation can proceed subsystem by subsystem, each subsystem relatively independent of the others. Whether agents or humans are doing the work, a good design makes the system much easier to understand, iterate on, validate and extend. As you learn the limitations of the design, you also now have the ability to redo it much more rapidly than ever before. Regardless of how much depth you decide to maintain in your projects, I’d make sure the broader structure continues to make sense. Additional reading There are several interesting articles, talks and books that are relevant: Addy Osmani with several additional techniques Guy Levi recommending leaning into critical thinking Cory Doctorow talking about handling being forced to use AI Stuart Halloway emphasizing that AI is automation, and the importance of friction to build metis . Elizabeth, SigNoz on skills atrophying. Ricard Solé et al. on LLMs as a cognitive virus, modeling the interaction and consequences of cognitive offloading. I’m curious if you have any other recommendations around effectively leveraging agents without losing context – I’d love to hear about additional experiments to try or workflows to adopt! Particularly if you’ve successfully recovered projects that collapsed into slop. Discuss on Hacker News . I have constantly been expecting more software to fail under the weight of its own complexity. One of my hot takes is that this hasn’t happened at the scale and magnitude I expect yet because agents became smarter fast enough to keep up with the debt introduced by the previous generation. ↩︎ You’ll pry my weekly indulgence in The Great British Baking Show from my cold, dead hands. ↩︎ You could argue that this is a very “Individual Contributor” approach to building things, and that managers deal with this all the time. I’ll quote Andrew Grove on management: “delegation without follow-through is abdication” – you still need to engage to get the outcome you need. ↩︎

title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
body_text: HackerTube – karpathy karpathy Home Blog HackerTube 31 Oct, 2026 It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org ! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews , filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 EDIT : A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.   Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

title: European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative
body_text: ERICI — European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative ERICI Why now The gap Reference stack Join European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative RISC-V Industrial Computers. Open, partitioned, built to last. RVA23 silicon has arrived. The industrial computer built on it has not. ERICI coordinates a reference stack, from firmware to real-time and general-purpose operating systems: it fixes the interfaces between the layers and verifies that they boot together on real RVA23 hardware. A box that boots it is ERICI-compatible . Non-commercial RVA23 Based in Europe, open worldwide Join the initiative ▶ Demonstration Linux operator GUI, HMI QSOE real-time control gRouvr partitioning hypervisor mr-bml boot loader, OS selection HFI BIOS firmware, Set-Up, boot control RVA23 RISC-V SoC cores, memory, devices, IOMMU The ERICI reference stack, tested together layer by layer. See how it boots Why now Industrial computing is ready for RISC-V Today's industrial computers run on x86 and Arm: two instruction sets, each owned and licensed by a single company. RISC-V is open, governed by a non-profit, and implemented by many vendors. Until recently it lacked what industrial systems need. That has changed. 1 An open ISA No license for the instruction set, no single owner, no single country. A machine expected to run for 15 years should not depend on one company's roadmap, or one government's decisions. 2 RVA23: a real baseline The RVA23 profile, ratified in October 2024, makes the hypervisor and vector extensions mandatory. Software can rely on them on every compliant chip. 3 Silicon is shipping The first RVA23 SoCs and boards are available in 2026, with eight 64-bit cores and an IOMMU. Developers can buy them today. 4 One box instead of two A partitioning hypervisor runs real-time control and the operator's Linux side by side, isolated from each other, on one SoC. From a university project to industrial computing 2010 RISC-V starts at UC Berkeley 2015 RISC-V Foundation founded 2020 RISC-V International, based in Switzerland 2021 Hypervisor and vector extensions ratified 2024 RVA23 profile ratified 2026 First RVA23 boards. ERICI starts. So why are there no RISC-V industrial computers yet? Board makers wait for software, software waits for boards, and customers wait for both. ERICI breaks that loop with an open reference stack running on real hardware. The gap The silicon is here. The industrial computer isn't yet. The first RVA23 machines are on the market: eight 64-bit RISC-V cores, the hypervisor extension, an IOMMU. They are excellent development and edge platforms. An industrial computer has to do more: survive the control cabinet, talk to the field, and stay available for a decade or longer. Firefly AIBOX-K3 T-Chip Intelligent Technology · edge mini PC SpacemiT K3, 8× X100 RISC-V cores up to 2.4 GHz, RVA23 Up to 32 GB LPDDR5, UFS, M.2 NVMe 2× Gigabit Ethernet, 9–20 V DC input −20 to 60 °C operating temperature Image © T-Chip Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. · product page Milk-V Jupiter2 Milk-V · single-board computer, metal case SpacemiT K3, 8× X100 RISC-V cores up to 2.4 GHz, RVA23 Up to 32 GB LPDDR5, UFS, M.2 NVMe Gigabit and 10 GbE SFP+, Wi-Fi 6 Real-time I/O expansion for EtherCAT and CAN-FD modules Image © Milk-V · product page What a RISC-V Industrial Computer needs Requirement AIBOX-K3 Jupiter2 RVA23 SoC with hypervisor extension and IOMMU Yes Yes 24 V DC supply, wide input range 9–20 V 12 V / USB-PD Extended temperature, −40 to 85 °C −20 to 60 °C Not stated Fieldbus and real-time I/O (EtherCAT, CAN, TSN) Not stated Via modules DIN-rail or panel mounting Not stated Not stated Hardware watchdog, isolated digital I/O Not stated Not stated Industrial EMC and safety certification Not stated Not stated Long-term availability, 10–15 years Not stated Not stated Partitioned software stack: real-time next to Linux Not yet Not yet Partitioned stack: demonstrated on the SpacemiT K3 PicoITX board, not yet on these products. See the video . Specifications as published by the manufacturers, October 2026. Both products are shown as examples of RVA23 hardware available today. No affiliation with ERICI or endorsement by the manufacturers is implied. The missing pieces are not the cores. They are the industrial hardware around them and an open, partitioned software stack on top. That is where ERICI starts. Reference stack Defined together, verified together A RISC-V Industrial Computer is built in layers. ERICI defines a reference stack, documents the interface between each pair of layers, and verifies the whole stack on real RVA23 hardware. The reference components are developed by QSOE Systems; Linux by its community. Each layer depends only on what the layer below hands over. Layer In the reference stack Interface below Operator partition GUI, HMI, networking Linux a general-purpose OS for everything that is not time-critical devicetree kernel + initrd Real-time partition control loops, machine I/O QSOE a QNX-style environment: /N on its own Skimmer microkernel, /L on seL4, same userspace devicetree kernel + initrd Multiboot3 for /L, next gRouvr Partitioning CPUs, memory, devices, IOMMU gRouvr --> gRouvr RVA23 resource-partitioning hypervisor; every available means of isolation, IOMMU included kernel + initrd, like Linux Loading boot menu, OS images mr-bml menu-driven boot loader: the operator selects which systems to start UEFI application Firmware initialization, boot control HFI BIOS U-Boot-based, with POST and a BIOS-style Set-Up for industrial boards RVA23 profile Hardware RVA23 SoC with IOMMU SpacemiT K3 8× X100 cores, hypervisor extension, IOMMU the silicon itself How it boots The firmware initializes the system, runs POST and offers its Set-Up . Then it starts a UEFI boot loader, and its job is done. The loader starts operating systems, or a hypervisor together with them. gRouvr is loaded just like a Linux kernel with its initrd. Its boot package is a CPIO archive that holds the kernel and initramfs image of every partition. So mr-bml loads it, and so does GRUB. gRouvr then gives each partition its own CPUs, memory and devices, and a devicetree that describes them. Real-time and Linux partitions start side by side. ▶ Watch the demonstration gRouvr booting Linux and QSOE/N on the SpacemiT K3. Opens on YouTube. Built to outlast Not tied to one chip The first RVA23 SoCs come from Chinese vendors; more will follow from other vendors and other regions. The reference stack depends on the RVA23 profile and on open interfaces, not on a particular SoC. Moving a box to another RVA23 chip means porting the firmware, adapting the hypervisor and the board's drivers. The real-time application and the operator's Linux move with it. Not tied to one developer The reference stack is open source: HFI BIOS under GPL-2.0, like the U-Boot it is based on; mr-bml under GPL-3.0; gRouvr and QSOE under Apache 2.0. Anyone can build, audit and maintain it, with or without its original developers. A machine that runs for 15 years needs software that can be maintained for 15 years. Join Build the RISC-V industrial computer with us ERICI is in its founding phase. Companies and institutions that see RVA23 as the future of industrial computing are welcome to join now and shape the initiative from the start. Who we invite, and what they bring Industrial hardware makers the box itself: an RVA23 board in a real enclosure, with I/O and a datasheet Silicon vendors RVA23 SoCs with an IOMMU and long-term availability Machine builders and plant operators requirements from the field, and a first machine to put a box in OS and driver vendors your RTOS, Linux distribution or drivers, brought up on a named RVA23 box Universities and research teaching and theses on real ERICI systems How ERICI works Non-commercial. ERICI sells nothing and charges no membership fees. Open interfaces. How each layer hands over to the next is public: UEFI, kernel + initrd, devicetree. Closed-source components are welcome, as long as they keep to these interfaces. Bring a real system. Contributions are RISC-V industrial computers: a named SoC in a real box, with a datasheet and a date. Software counts when it serves such a system, such as the driver that lets the real-time partition on box X run its machine. Concrete, not abstract. No road maps without silicon, no specs without a system that boots them. Interested? Let's talk. contact@erici.eu Initiated by Yuri Zaporozhets · Ravensburg, Germany ERICI · European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative · non-commercial QSOE HFI BIOS gRouvr --> Impressum Privacy
