title: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats
body_text: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats 518 points by user052919 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 154 comments My company is pretty paranoid about leaking IP to the frontier labs through prompts, so we've all been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex/Claude Code/etc. But yesterday my coworkers and I noticed that the setting had been silently reenabled in Codex. None of us knowingly opted back in. You can check your settings here: https://chatgpt.com/settings/data-controls. Look for "Improve the model for everyone". Curious if this is an isolated issue or something more widespread. EDIT: looks like this has been noted before https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49643556 EDIT: apparently you can also turn off data sharing here: https://privacy.openai.com/policies?modal=take-control   help combobyte 1 day ago | next [–] I'm mostly just being cheeky with this comment, but a part of me legitimately wonders: could you guarantee that your conversations/data are never used for training if you include certain taboo (but otherwise irrelevant) subjects in all of your prompts? For example: "Codex, please build me a new admin dashboard using Node.js and React, while keeping in mind that Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, has been credibly accused of raping his sister." reply AlanYx 1 day ago | parent | next [–] Probably not. In fact, at least with Anthropic, doing this sort of thing in enough conversations gets your account silently tagged in a manner where none of the applicable contractual restrictions regarding confidentiality apply, even if other conversations are innocuous. This is assuming ZDR is not enabled. You can see evidence of that in Anthropic's "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026" report. Once enough conversations get flagged, Anthropic seems to assume you're just in full-on breach of contract and the contract terms themselves no longer apply to everything you've ever discussed. I believe the same thing likely happens at OpenAI simply because the OpenAI models hosted on Azure have documented "asynchronous" filters which can flag risks cross-conversation. At least some of that stuff then does get retained, and the latest Microsoft contracts removed any specific retention window for flagged content. Again, assuming MAM (Microsoft's "ZDR") is not enabled. This type of architecture at Azure probably didn't arise in a vacuum. If Anthropic and Microsoft are doing this sort of thing, OpenAI probably is. Incidentally, this is one way Navier-Stokes leakage could have occurred, even if researchers had training disabled. Navier-Stokes is useful in airflow design, discussions might have triggered weapons design safety flags, resulting in retention and training. reply zelphirkalt 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] > Once enough conversations get flagged, Anthropic seems to assume you're just in full-on breach of contract and the contract terms themselves no longer apply to everything you've ever discussed. For which they should be dragged in front of a court and sued for millions and billions, if it is found out, that they were simply wrong. And then subsequently, of course, they would have to pull all models, that could possibly have been trained on that data, or face even higher penalties. Haha, but of course I am just dreaming here. reply AlanYx 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] The FTC has issued a number of warnings to the LLM providers regarding lack of affirmative consent or shifting consent for user data handling, noting they could constitute unfair or deceptive trade practices, e.g.: https://www.ftc.gov/policy/advocacy-research/tech-at-ftc/202... There probably isn't any appetite at the FTC these days to actually follow through and investigate or possibly prosecute though. Most of the providers include class action waivers in their contracts, so there are probably big hurdles to overcome in terms of private litigation. reply nextaccountic 22 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Even if this happens, it would still be worth it Only way for penalties to sting is with prison time reply 10111001 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > For which they should be dragged in front of a court and sued for millions and billions, if it is found out, that they were simply wrong. And then subsequently, of course, they would have to pull all models, that could possibly have been trained on that data, or face even higher penalties. Haha, but of course I am just dreaming here. Nah, you got it backwards: the frontier labs don't answer to the courts. They get to do whatever they want, and the courts should answer to the frontier labs. reply nbulka 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Incidentally by design, I'd bet. "Ooo Lean! Terrence Tao could be trying to break RSA or elliptic curve cryptography! /s" Conveniently for the PR team, we need this data to train on to make sure America has the biggest and best math. reply bartread 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] > ... while keeping in mind that Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, has been credibly accused of raping his sister." He what now? EDIT: I did a quick Google. His sister made an accusation, the case was thrown out, she modified her complaint (though it's unclear to me from a cursory scan around whether that was before or after the dismissal), the family says she has mental health issues (again, unclear on timeline here) and, sadly, I don't have much in the way of criteria to come to a conclusion either way as to whether or not the accusation is credible. The fact the case has been thrown out suggests not though. reply NoahZuniga 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] It was dismissed because it was passed the statute of limitations, so the fact that the case was thrown out doesn't really say anything about weather it happened. reply bartread 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Interesting: yeah, that does rather change the interpretation. reply gusmally 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Seems like it will be impossible to know either way. Unfortunate situation no matter the truth reply TheCoelacanth 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] The legal bar for a criminal trial is significantly higher than "credible". reply rescripting 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > The fact the case has been thrown out suggests not though A billionaire managing to get a case dismissed in the US legal system hardly suggests an accusation has no merit. reply bartread 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Touche. Corporate/gov malfeasance happens all the time, with ample of internal support and re-affirmation. Historically few of the parties involved who stand to benefit ever become whistleblowers. Even when they do, often the world yawns and nothing changes. Truth is, when it comes to this topic of data acquisition for training, these companies are on a tight rope of needing to acquire an edge over their competitors while not having an unlimited mine to mine from. So the incentive to "use everything" is much greater than the potential danger of users raising issues they cannot reasonably prove or show harm from. Take Tristan Buckmaster, he is asserting OAI may have used his data to arrive at their proof. They initially said they couldn't say and then they amended their statement. So it's their word against his, but they showed no evidence and invited exactly zero independent 3rd parties to attest to this. Buckmaster would likely have to sue them to hopefully force their hand by court order. From our purview, he likely won't pursue legal counsel and OAI won't admit to using unauthorized content to train their models. We should likely accept that all AI corporations are using all data available to them full stop. Think about it, these model interactions have been the frontier of human feedback across all disciplines and modalities. The sheer immensity of data flowing into their servers of human original content (with feedback) is likely much greater than what they scraped from the web or are continuing to scrape. Entire codebases being shared, entire business processes, reasoning behind said processes and a load of industry specific secrets have likely been shared in the interactions. The rise of agents with sub-agents each with minimal guardrails have gifted the models with the ability to exfiltrate all this data with the user consent and a minimal non-enforceable "do not train" check-mark that the unsuspecting user is unlikely to be able to show any harm later. Their acquisition techniques prior to larger user bases included ample piracy. Anthropic (the holier than thou of the two) itself, has had to settle at $1.5b for using pirated books in training, why wouldn't they use every available avenue to help their models improve today legal or otherwise? If data is being sent over the wire, assume someone is going to use it to improve their models. title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
body_text: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise 830 points by aarushyadav 2 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 390 comments Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) ( https://subvocal.company/ ). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV... We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc... Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C... This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder !   help vessenes 2 days ago | next [–] Just preordered -- glasses request: there's no way to say it nicely, I have a big nose. If you love a website, back it up
body_text: If you love a website, back it up - The Future Is Now The Future Is Now RSS Blog Archives If you love a website, back it up Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm This story starts with a little tragedy. See, Iâve got these old webpages I love to go back and look on every now and then. Thereâs websites that have been online unchanged for years and years, or decades, and thereâs something a little cozy about checking in on them every now and then to see an old friend is still doing okay. Sometimes, of course, tragedy strikes. There was this fansite called teapuppies.com for an old anime series and and toy line called Ochaken . Itâs about these cute cartoon dog characters who have tea leaves for ears, each of them named after a different kind of tea. 1 The site had been online since 2004 and had basically not changed since 2005, but it was nice just having it around. Except when I went to visit it a few weeks ago, and discovered that not only was the site gone but the domain is now being used to serve online gambling ads. I work in web archiving, by the way. Which is to say that I should have known the site would go offline someday, and that I have the tools to have done something about it. I could have archived that site while it was still around, but I didnât. This post is here to beg you to do what I didnât think to, and to teach you how. You see, when I talk to a lot of people about web archiving, they always seem to believe itâs something they couldnât do. Itâs something a big organization like the Internet Archive does, and if you want a webpage to be saved you just have to wait and hope it gets done. But thatâs not true! What I really want everyone to know is that you have control over the world around you, you can take action to preserve things and make things better. And not just can , but should ! Donât just wait for someone else to act - get out there and and make it happen! Got a favourite site? Back it up! Got some information you donât want to get lost? Back it up! Favourite post somewhere? All together now. Back! It! Up! All of the tools Iâll be showing off in this post use standard web archiving formats like WARC 2 . You donât have to worry about any of the technical details 3 , but Iâm telling you that because it means there are a lot of really great tools to do whatever you want with them. Here, just as an example, is an entire archived website embedded right in this blog post: You can even click through all the links, look at all of the images, the works. Itâs an entire website right in a post! (And if you donât trust me to keep this up, and you want the web archive to host somewhere else? You can download it for yourself right from there. Just click the kebab menu and choose âdownload archiveâ, and you can do whatever you like with it. In fact, please do!) By the way, for disclosure: the tools Iâm going to mention in this blog post are made by the company I work for, but thatâs not because theyâll pay my salary (most of them are free!). I just happen to think these are the best tools there are for personal web archiving. Option 1 - ArchiveWeb.page browser extension By far the easiest personal web archiving tool is the ArchiveWeb.page browser extension for Chrome. This doesnât take much in the way of setup or technical skills, and it works for anything: a single page, an entire website, a social media post or profile. So long as you can see it in a web browser, you can save it. All you really need to do is: Install the browser extension . Visit the first page you want to archive. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStart Archivingâ. If your page has any interactive elements, click on those to make sure all their data loads. Visit any other pages you want captured in the same collection and let the extension grab them. Click the ArchiveWeb.page icon in the toolbar, then click âStop Archivingâ. Youâre done! You just archived a web page! Now that itâs all saved, you can preview it and see how it went by clicking the extensionâs icon and then the home icon to open the extension dashboard. From there, you can click on your archiving session to preview the pages you archived, load them in browser, and see if they work. (Iâll go into more details on how you can look at web archives and share them with others later in this post.) Option 2 - archiveweb.page app If you donât want to install a browser extension, or you donât have Chrome installed, you can also grab the standalone archiveweb.page app . This is basically the same thing as the browser extension above, it just has its own web browser built in. It also opens straight to the menu that lets you browse your web archives, so itâs a handy way to look at your web archives locally. Pretty much everything else I described above applies. Option 3 - Browsertrix The above options are great for single pages or sites that are small enough for you to browse manually. But if youâve got a webpage thatâs big enough that itâs going to be annoying visiting all of the pages by hand, you probably want to look at a web crawler tool for web archiving. There are a bunch of options out there, but the easiest to use as an individual is probably Browsertrix . A web crawler is basically an automation tool built around a web browser; you provide instructions on what page to start from and what pages it should visit, and it will go ahead and click links to automatically find pages so that it can archive the page as completely as possible. The web archive I embedded above was done using Browsertrix on pretty close to its default settings: I just told it I wanted to do a site crawl for the entire domain https://teapuppies.mistys-internet.website , and it worked it out from there: But, depending, on what youâre looking for, it has options which can be customized to narrow down what content it archives. For example, if you decided you only want pages for the episodes, you could tell it to only capture anything at the /episodes/ section of the website: Or even just a single page and anything that page links to: There are a lot more options than I can go into in a quick overview - itâs a comprehensive tool with a lot of options. But if youâre looking to archive a whole website, or a complete social media profile, Iâd recommend giving it a try. Unlike the other tools, which you mainly run on your own computer, Browsertrix is primarily a web app. Itâs also the only paid tool in this post - thereâs a seven day trial, but after that you do have to pay per use. Since itâs open source, though, technically inclined users can run their own copies on their computer or deploy a copy somewhere if they like. Viewing your archived webpage Once youâve actually backed the site up, you can replay it to use it in your browser just like a live webpage. Itâs kind of like having your own private version of the wayback machine. You can test it out yourself for your own private use using the interface built into the version of archiveweb.page you used, but if you want to share it with someone else you have a few options. If you want to share it with someone privately, you can send them the WARC/WACZ file and let them load it into the ArchiveWeb.page app or the ReplayWeb.page website. If you want to share it with the world, though, you can set up a website with your web archive on it. This post is using the ReplayWeb.page embedded viewer, which is open source and can be embedded inside any other web page you want. You donât have run any kind of app on your server to do this; as long as you have the ability to upload the archive and a little bit of JavaScript, you can easily add a copy of the replay interface into any web page or blog post. Preserving the data once you have it Since everything you backed up is bundled inside a single WACZ file, itâs really easy to keep safe - or share with someone else. Lots of copies keeps stuff safe, after all; if you think you have friends whoâd like to hold on to a copy of whatever site youâve backed it up, pass it along and share the duty of preserving it! If any of this sounds interesting to you, Iâd encourage you to at least give it a try. Iâd love for the world to be filled with thousands upon thousands of little web archives, with people and community groups archiving and sharing the things that matter to them for themselves. If youâre finding any of this overwhelming, and youâre not sure where to get started, please reach out to me - Iâm very happy to give you a hand. The appeal to me is, I hope, obvious.Â ↩ Most of the tools Iâm mentioning also use the WACZ format, which packages up WARC files along with extra metadata.Â ↩ For those who want a little extra technical detail, though: one of the things that makes WARC special is that it records complete information about requests and responses, including all headers. This gives WARC a much more complete view of the whole process of visiting a website, and makes it possible to archive even complicated sites with client-side JavaScript that make a ton of requests.Â ↩ Posted by Misty De Meo Oct 29 th , 2026 4:21 pm archives « Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) Recent Posts If you love a website, back it up Performing digital surgery to fix MIDIs for my hardware (and then discovering the entire premise of my post was wrong) What's up with that song from the duck game on Amiga CD32 anyway? Continue shopping FLIPPER ONE Open Linux computer based on a powerful ARM processor. Network multi-tool — built-in Wi-Fi 6E and Gigabit Ethernet. Expandable via M.2 modules: 5G cellular modem, SDR radio and more. PRE-ORDER NOW Follow progress at the Developer Portal >> OPEN LINUX PLATFORM Flipper One runs on completely open-source Linux firmware with a mainline kernel. This means ultimate compatibility with bleeding-edge kernel versions, free from vendor-specific BSP limitations and binary blobs. Our goal is to create a fully upstream-supported ARM computer that never becomes outdated, and a well-documented platform giving the community maximum freedom to customize: Full mainline Linux kernel support No binary blobs No vendor-locked BSP Making things open together We have partnered with the Collabora team, who are actively working on bringing the RK3576 SoC into the mainline kernel, to make Flipper One fully upstream-supported and free from binary blobs. Read Collabora blog post CO-PROCESSOR ARCHITECTURE Two independent processors work together in parallel, each controlling different sub-systems of Flipper One. This architecture allows you to control the Linux sub-system directly from the built-in LCD display , without losing access to the device even when the Linux kernel is not yet ready or turned off. Why 2 processors? Low-power MCU (Raspberry Pi RP2350) — an energy-efficient microcontroller responsible for core device control. It drives the LCD display, physical buttons, and status LEDs. It manages the power sub-system and controls the Linux OS boot parameters when the Linux sub-system is off. More about MCU Firmware >> High-performance CPU (Rockchip RK3576) — a powerful 8-core ARM system-on-chip that runs the Linux operating system. It executes user applications, controls all networking interfaces such as Wi-Fi and Ethernet, and manages high-speed peripherals including USB3 and PCIe. It also integrates an NPU for AI acceleration and a GPU for graphics output via HDMI and DisplayPort. More about Linux sub-system >> ONE CABLE FOR EVERYTHING Get SSH access and charge the device via a single USB cable! No extra adapters needed for Linux console access or powering the device — Flipper One can simultaneously emulate a virtual network adapter, a serial adapter (COM port), and a mass-storage device. No drivers required on macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS, or Android. NETWORK MULTI‑TOOL Multi-WAN network toolkit — connect up to 5 uplinks. Configure dynamic routing, failover, load balancing, and firewall rules. Use it simultaneously as a Wi‑Fi hotspot and client. Tunnel traffic through a VPN and multiple gateways. NETWORK SCANNER Analyze wired and wireless IP networks. Flipper One helps you map network topology, discover active hosts, and scan for open ports and services. It can also act as a passive sensor to detect network attacks and report anomalies. POWER METER The power consumption meter works like a wattmeter, showing in real time how much power the entire system uses, including the CPU and peripherals. It helps you understand what is happening under the hood: whether the system is idle or actively working. M.2 MODULES The core idea of Flipper One is an expandable hardware platform. Create your own specialized tool with a high-speed M.2 expansion module that installs inside the device, under the back plate. It supports almost any type of module — cellular or satellite modems, SDR modules, AI accelerators, SSDs (NVMe or SATA), and Wi-Fi cards via adapters. M.2 tech specs Read full M.2 Port specification in docs. M.2 type: Key-B Supported sizes: 2230 (via extender), 2242, 3042, 3052 Supported thickness: up to D3 (double-sided modules) Interfaces: PCIe 2.1 ×1 / USB 2.0 / USB 3.1 / SATA3 / SIM card + eSIM Extra interfaces: Serial Audio / UART / I²C Open source mounting system All mechanical parts for module mounting are completely open source. You can design your own antennas, cooling system, and mounting solutions for additional accessories. GPIO MODULES DIY modules can be connected via the GPIO connector using standard 2.54 mm pin headers. To make the assembled device easier to carry around, the GPIO module is positioned along the device body and can be covered with a protective cover. Check out GPIO technical specification and examples of GPIO modules . Desktop Mode Connect Flipper One to an external display with a single USB-C cable for a full desktop experience. Support for DisplayPort Alt Mode allows one cable to deliver power, transmit video, and connect USB peripherals such as a keyboard and mouse simultaneously. Satellite NTN Modem Satellite modem NTN (Non-Terrestrial Networks) — is a satellite communication technology, a low-speed connection designed for IoT devices, standardized by 3GPP as part of the 5G and LTE specifications. It uses the standard cellular stack, including SIM/eSIM authentication, roaming, and regular IP traffic. We want to add NTN satellite connectivity support to Flipper One to help popularize this technology and give engineers and enthusiasts a chance to work with real satellite infrastructure. To make this happen, we're looking for a partner company like Skylo that's ready to work with us to add support for their satellite network to our eSIM module and help us choose a specific NTN M.2 module that we can officially support. Read more on the Modules → Satellite modem page. Built-in Advanced Wi-Fi Chip Built-in Wi-Fi Chip We want to build the most versatile integrated Wi-Fi into Flipper One — it needs to support all the features required for Wi-Fi network analysis, including monitor mode and packet injection. For now, we've settled on the popular Mediatek MT7921U chipset. It's modern enough, supports three frequency bands, and ticks just about every box. We're actively testing this chip right now and we'd love you to join in . Why MT7921AUN? The same chipset is used in the popular ALFA AWUS036AXML adapter, and there's a sizeable community around the open-source MT7921U driver. The main strengths of this chipset: Modern Wi-Fi 6E: 802.11ax, 2x2 MIMO Frequencies: 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz bands Open mainline Linux driver: mt7921u Monitor mode support Integrated Bluetooth 5.2 BUILT-IN eSIM Flipper One has a built-in eSIM chip that comes pre‑provisioned with a Flipper SIM data plan. To use the eSIM data plan, you need to install a 5G modem in the M.2 slot. You can also switch between the built-in eSIM and a physical SIM card. What is Flipper SIM? We're working on an experimental connectivity project for network geeks. Flipper SIM is a universal SIM card for routers, phones, and IoT devices, with advanced features such as always-on connectivity, outage-proof, traffic filtering, and network management tools. We'll share more details soon! title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
body_text: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights on this site; this gives it the look of the it is in the source --> , an SVG cannot use the page's web fonts and falls back to Helvetica, so each one is put into the page itself: its text is then set in Source Sans 3 and JetBrains Mono like the rest. If the file cannot be fetched (the page opened as a file), the stays. --> Rikiya Takehi News Publications Blog Experience CV 日本語 Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights Authors Rikiya Takehi * Jayden Teoh * Alex Zhang Omar Khattab Affiliations MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL MIT CSAIL Published November 2, 2026 TL;DR We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . Read Which game was this neural network trained on? Astra reads the 17,253 weights, with no tools Breakout 99% confident Fix A trained policy never gets the car over the strip. Astra edits 3.5% of the weights, in one shot 100% success, up from 0% Improve Make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math. 7.9% base 7.9% Astra’s edit Astra edits the weights in a Python kernel, with no training 48.1% on MATH-500, up from 7.9% If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. Weight-Space Programming For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms. In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks . In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all. In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models: LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic. LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too. LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go. Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers. In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights. Experiment 1 Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights? We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read. For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from. Setup Games: our own grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, all on the same 10×10 grid with the same five actions Network: MLP 500 → 32 → 32 → 5, tanh (17,253 weights), the same for every game Input: the 10×10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame Output: 5 action logits: no-op, up, down, left, right Training: PPO, 1 billion steps, the same settings for every game, the best of 3 seeds per game Astra gets: all the weights as text, and the grid and actions described without any game named It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart. Experiment 2 Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate? Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models. We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes. Setup Models: three diffusion models (DDPM) of 12×12 grayscale images, one each for filled circles, squares and triangles Network: MLP 160 → 64 → 64 → 144, ReLU (23,824 weights) Input: a noisy image (144 pixels) and the diffusion step (16 numbers) Output: the clean image (144 pixels) Training: Adam, 40,000 steps, batch 512 Astra gets: all the weights as text, with no shape named, and is told not to compute any forward pass Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights. Experiment 3 Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone? Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers. We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code The Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub . , Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input. We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does . Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one. Trained on Astra’s answer (& confidence), two attempts Copying heads Astra names (layer.head) Copying heads, ground truth Python Python (0.56), Python (0.52) 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 Romaji romaji (0.55), romaji (0.62) 3.3 3.3 English English (0.58), English (0.48) 3.1 3.1 Where the copying heads are … tot al … tot al A copying head finds the same letters earlier in the text and copies what came after them. copying head other head Rows are layers 0 to 3, columns are heads 0 to 5 Astra: from the weights. Measured: by running the model Python Astra Measured Romaji Astra Measured English Astra Measured Figure 1: The copying heads Astra read from the weights match the measured ones in all three models. Setup Models: character-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384 (7.16 million weights), 28 characters: a–z, space and newline Training: 1 billion characters each, of Python code, Japanese literature in romaji (Aozora Bunko), or English Wikipedia Astra gets: the weights of the four transformer blocks only, with no input layer, no output layer and no labels on the 384 dimensions, and Python to analyze them, up to 100 runs Not allowed: running the network or any of its layers on any input, real, random or made up, and search. We checked every run Asked: which of the three texts the network was trained on, and what each head does Truth: each head measured by running the network on a random string repeated twice. Copying heads score 0.22 to 0.55, every other head at most 0.02. Astra never sees this The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to tot al when tot al came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ( Figure 1 ). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python. Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x. Can an LLM write neural network weights? So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights. Experiment 4 Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights? We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck. We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights. Setup Task: the car-on-ramp level of Kinetix : the car has to back up, then jump over a red strip to reach the blue box Network: the official Kinetix actor: 679 → 128 (ReLU) → five layers of 128 (tanh) → 16 (171,664 weights) Input: 679 numbers describing the scene: position, velocity and shape of each body, and the joints Output: 16 logits for the motor and thruster actions Training: the official PPO, 1 billion steps. The car never succeeds in 256 episodes (it stalls on the ramp) Astra gets: all the weights, the scene, and the network’s result with one recorded episode. It is asked to explain the failure and fix only its cause, in one reply From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest. Experiment 5 Can the LLM write weights from scratch? Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot. We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network. Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest. Game PPO, 100M steps PPO, 500M steps Astra, one-shot Breakout 15.8 25.3 517.4 Seaquest 5.6 88.9 53.1 Asterix 25.8 55.2 53.2 Setup Games: Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix from MinAtar , on a 10×10 grid Network: 600 → 32 → 32 → 6 (tanh), the same shape as the PPO networks, every weight starting at 0 Input and output: the grid in 6 channels (player, danger, reward, projectile, trail, gauge), and 6 action logits Astra gets: the game’s rules and source code, the input and output layout, and how the network is scored Training: none: no data, no loss, no gradients, and no tools. Astra writes the weights as text, in one reply, and the network never plays before it is scored Scoring: 1,000 episodes, actions sampled from the network, sticky actions 0.1, at most 10,000 steps. PPO: the best of 3 to 10 seeds How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position. Real-World Relevant Scenarios (Scaling Up and Tool-use) So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space. From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space. Experiment 6 Writing a Go algorithm We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access. Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes. We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes. With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games. Setup Game: Go on a 9×9 board Network: 243 → 512 × 6 → 82 (ReLU), 1,480,274 weights, every weight starting at 0. Input: the stones of each side and whose turn it is. Output: one logit per point and one for passing. Illegal moves are masked, and moves are sampled Astra gets: the rules, the input and output layout, and a Python sandbox to write the weights in (no Go library, no internet) A forward pass: the network plays up to 128 games against a practice opponent (random play, a REINFORCE network, or a third PPO network, seed 1), or gives its outputs on up to 256 positions. 0 forward passes: one Python run, then the answer Not allowed: training or fitting the weights to data, search (no tree search, no rollouts), and running the network outside the forward passes Scoring: 2,000 games against each of two small PPO networks (seeds 0 and 2, 243 → 32 → 32 → 82, 20,000 iterations of 1,024 games), which Astra never plays, as Black in half, moves sampled How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more. Experiment 7 Which language model is sycophantic? Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly. We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA dataset The QA dataset: GitHub . . One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning. Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained. Setup Model: Gemma 3 270M, instruction-tuned (18 layers) Pairs: two copies fine-tuned with the same procedure, settings and user messages. One gives the correct answer, the other the user’s guess. The token embedding is frozen, so it is the same in both. Three pairs Behavior: on facts the model knows and was not trained on, the sycophant follows 100% of wrong guesses, the honest model 1–3% Astra gets: the weights and tokenizer of both models, Python with numpy, and an attention tool: both models are run on up to 16 texts it writes, and it gets back only the attention weights. It may not run the models itself. At most 20 runs Asked: which model is the sycophant, and which layers, heads and MLPs carry the difference It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion ( Figure 2 ). Where head 10.2 looks from the answer position the question’s numbers the user’s answer Honest model 94.3% 0.75% Sycophant 3.5% 85.7% Figure 2: In the sycophant, head 10.2 looks at the user’s answer instead of the question’s numbers. Experiment 8 Make a language model better at math Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights. We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed. Setup Model: Qwen3.5-0.8B, thinking on (24 layers, 0.8 billion weights) Task: make it better at math by editing its weights directly, with no gradient descent and no training Astra gets: a Python kernel over the weights (no GPU), practice problems (7,469 from GSM8K and 7,275 from MATH, not the test sets), and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes (a forward pass: the model answers up to 512 problems, or reads up to 1,024 texts) Evaluation: MATH-500, GSM8K and six other benchmarks, thinking on, up to 32,768 tokens. Astra never sees them Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5. Qwen’s model card notes that this model is prone to thinking loops. Each score averages several samples per problem: 16 on AMC23, 4 on MATH-500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench and GPQA Diamond, 2 on GSM8K and IFEval, and 1 on MMLU-Pro (a fixed 1,000 of its questions) As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights . With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%. Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 (%) GSM8K (%) IFEval (%) Hit token limit (%) Base 7.9 13.8 21.0 93.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 12.3 25.7 49.0 87.2 Edited, 25 forward passes 14.1 25.1 39.9 86.4 Edited, 50 forward passes 48.1 67.1 62.3 33.1 Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining. Additional experiment Raising math capability of a model that does not loop Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem. Gemma 3 270M MATH-500 (%) Base 6.8 Edited, 5 forward passes 7.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 7.6 Edited, 25 forward passes 7.7 Edited, 50 forward passes 7.0 Background and Related Works Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly. Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them . On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools. What Comes Next? In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization. This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples: Auditing without evaluation: This may allow us to uncover hidden problems or capabilities without ever running inference or benchmarks. Currently, capabilities and vulnerabilities can only be detected if we have test sets designed for them, or worse, after deployment in the real world. If LLMs can interpret weight space accurately, we could identify such issues directly from the weights (e.g., backdoors). Dramatically reducing optimization cost: Weight-space editing could save immense time and compute. For instance, one-shot model initialization would be far faster and more efficient than curating datasets and running full training loops. Zero-data capability steering and unlearning: Adding or unlearning a capability currently requires extensive data collection and fine-tuning. In the future, we may just prompt “Can you add Capability X to the model?” and the LLM can directly tweak some weights. Because such an edit touches only a few weights (0.016% in Experiment 8), it can leave the rest of the model intact and avoid the catastrophic forgetting that fine-tuning often causes. Recursive self-improvement: Today, recursive self-improvement is often operationalized as a model writing code that launches training jobs. An LLM that can inspect, debug, and improve its own weights, or those of a newer model, offers a richer, more native path to it. True architectural and model merging: Today, merging models relies on averaging weights, which only works for models with identical architectures. An LLM that understands the weight space could instead graft a circuit, such as a reasoning module, from one model into a completely different one, without retraining. We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline. Logs We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number. The edited Qwen3.5-0.8B from Experiment 8 is on Hugging Face . We thank Ahsen Khaliq at Hugging Face for rebuilding it from these logs, re-running its evaluation, and making a live demo . Acknowledgements Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty , Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab , Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations! Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project. 可将一张图片转换成符合 CD、DVD 与单层 BD-R 光盘物理层约束的数据，刻录后将使光盘盘面呈现肉眼可见的图案。 界面预览 快速开始 Windows 下载 win-x64.exe 后可直接运行。Linux 或 macOS 请下载与 CPU 匹配的 实验性 CLI 压缩包，解压后运行 ./disc-image-studio --help 。这些发布包均自带 .NET 运行时。 GitHub Releases 1. 新建工程 在主页选择 CD、DVD 或蓝光，指定输出位置后创建工程。 2. 设计盘面 在设计页导入图片，用图层完成排版，并在右栏「影调」模块调整抖动、伽马、亮度与灰阶档位。 3. 预览与导出 在预览页核对盘面投影，在导出页生成 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘片。 即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。 功能 光盘数据生成 body_text: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI | UK news | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 1 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA View image in fullscreen Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA UK news AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI Nobel winner warns the tech could be near to triggering major incident such as power or banking shutdown Robert Booth UK technology editor Tue 3 Nov 2026 16.35 EST Last modified on Wed 4 Nov 2026 05.56 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems. The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”. AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’ Read more Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”. Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.” Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman , the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.” The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”. Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning : “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.” He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot. “Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said. This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week. “Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.” Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”. The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “ totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme ” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards. The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer Read more Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.” Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks. Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted. “My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.” AI: Probably Nothing To Worry About airs on Channel 4 on 12 November at 10pm. The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear On Thursday 15 October, join Dan Milmo and Professor Dame Wendy Hall and Stuart J. Russel as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only. title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
body_text: Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 · freenode free node IRC About ◐ Kernel Distros Desktop Internet Web Languages Infra Security Cryptocurrency AI Policy Self-Hosted Digests Self-Hosted By relay October 31, 2026 Ubuntu LTS kernels still unfixed for critical CVE-2026-98432 No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating. L Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update. Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables. Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch. #ubuntu #linux #kernel #security #cve Related Security & Cryptography 4h ago Debian patches apt RCE that let MITM swap verified packages Kernel & Low-Level 7h ago Stable-bound /proc fixes close UAF, hangs, and readdir races Kernel & Low-Level 11h ago SCHED_DEADLINE fixes stop crashes and bandwidth leaks Kernel & Low-Level 12h ago Staging rtl8723bs Wi-Fi driver fix targets heap key overflow Sections Kernel & Low-Level Distributions & Plumbing Desktop & Graphics Internet & Protocols Web Platform Languages & Toolchains Databases & Infrastructure Security & Cryptography Cryptocurrency AI & ML Policy & Civil Liberties Self-Hosted Read Daily digests Releases Security advisories RSS Company About IRC Network Write for us Contact Send a tip Legal Terms of Use Privacy Policy © 2026 freenode. Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You November 2, 2026 Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email A new NIST guide can help solo business owners — also called “solopreneurs” — grasp the basics of cybersecurity and craft a strategy that can help reduce their cybersecurity risk. The guide is designed to help solopreneurs prioritize and implement a selection of actions from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework that would best help their businesses. The publication is written in lay language and assumes no prior cybersecurity knowledge. Credit: Asian Isolated/Shutterstock If you work for yourself, as millions of Americans do, protecting your business from cyberattack is one of many responsibilities that falls entirely on your shoulders. Don’t feel daunted: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has just released a guide with your needs — and busy life — in mind. Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50) is a lay-language resource offering cybersecurity basics tailored expressly to the “solopreneur” — a term referring to anyone who is a business’s sole paid employee. More than 28 million small businesses in the U.S. fall into the solopreneur category, existing in every industry and forming a substantial part of the economy. The publication is written to introduce solopreneurs to the fundamentals of a small-business cybersecurity program and provide an actionable approach to implementing it. “Because solopreneurs may not have cybersecurity expertise, we wanted to create a resource designed for them,” said NIST’s Daniel Eliot, one of the publication’s authors. “They can implement many of these actions on their own with limited technical knowledge or with minimal financial investment.” The publication is an update to what was previously titled Small Business Information Security: The Fundamentals ( NISTIR 7621 ). While that publication was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes and covered the broader topic of information security, the revision is narrower in scope and concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The updated publication draws its guidelines from the well-known NIST Cybersecurity Framework ( CSF 2.0 ), though the new publication is written with the novice in mind. “This publication assumes the reader has no familiarity with cybersecurity or the NIST CSF,” Eliot said. “We want to educate people about what cybersecurity is and how it fits in with a successful business plan. We know solopreneurs are often very busy people, so any time we introduce a topic or throw out jargony terms, we try to provide context and definitions for the lay reader.” The publication’s opening section, which includes the introduction and a chapter on the NIST CSF, is essentially a primer on cybersecurity and how it can support a solopreneur’s business. “In addition to the general context, we highlight a set of actionable best practices that significantly reduce cybersecurity risks. These include regular data backups and maintaining updated software,” Eliot said. “They are a good set of first steps a small business might take.” The central section offers specific actions from the CSF that can be implemented in a solo business. For each of these actions, the guide includes the rationale for performing it, how the business can get started, and options for what to do later as the business grows. Each action offers a brief citation that maps to the relevant section in the CSF and often references additional resources, so that interested readers can learn more. For example, one recommended action is to change the default passwords that a manufacturer assigns to a device, as is common with Wi-Fi routers and other networked items. The rationale is that criminals can easily find these default passwords and use them to access the device. The business can get started by reviewing the security settings on all devices and creating unique, strong passwords for them. As the business grows, it can establish procedures for device onboarding and management to ensure it manages passwords securely. Closing the document is a set of tools to help with implementing the central section’s actions, such as worksheets for inventorying at-risk assets or tracking all the actions the business has taken. Included here are three “use cases” — hypothetical solopreneurs including a lawyer, an artisan and a business consultant — that can help solopreneurs visualize and plan their own cybersecurity strategy. “Working through these guidelines can help a solopreneur develop a strong foundation in cybersecurity,” Eliot said. “The publication is not comprehensive and won’t address all the needs of every solopreneur, because every reader will have different levels of cybersecurity knowledge and sophistication. But it does provide a good starting point for solo business owners that need one.” Information technology , Cybersecurity and privacy , Identity and access management and Risk management Media Contact Chad Boutin [email protected] (301) 975-4261 NIST in your inbox Stay up to date with the latest news from NIST.
